blocks.title: Sliding Window: the k closest values, and which window when
blocks.builds_on: Days 26 to 30 · Sliding Window, and Days 19 to 25 · Two Pointers
points: Today's window has a fixed size k, like Day 26's, but you don't want a summary of every window: the window's position is the answer. You slide it to find the best place for it.

Two ways to place it. Slide: move the window one step at a time and update the score from only what changed, the item that left and the one that entered, since everything in between is shared. Or close in from both ends, as on Day 19, dropping one end at a time and saying each time why the end you drop can't be in the answer (Day 25).

Today closes the topic, so here it is on one screen. Fixed size: update a summary with one item in and one out (Day 26, Contains Duplicate II). A left end that jumps when no earlier start can win (Day 27, Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock).
Longest valid window: grow on the right, shrink while the rule is broken, record after shrinking (Day 29, Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters and Longest Repeating Character Replacement).

Fixed windows that compare letter counts, with a running number of matched letters as the fast version (Day 30, Permutation in String). Shortest valid window: grow until valid, then record inside the shrink loop (Day 30, Minimum Size Subarray Sum).

Spotting a window problem: the question is about neighbouring items (a substring or subarray), and a valid window stays valid when it shrinks (Day 29's property). If negative numbers break that, use prefix sums and a dict instead (Day 18).

find-k-closest-elements: For today's problem, decide which of the two fits and what makes one choice better than another. Write that rule in one line before coding, including what happens on a tie.
Day 32 starts Binary Search. Once you have done Day 32, try today's problem again as a challenge: can a binary search find where the best window starts? You don't need it today.

blocks.say: When the window's size is fixed but its place is the answer, I slide it and update from only what left and what entered, or close in from both ends dropping an end that can't be in the answer, so it stays O(n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): delivery stops along a road at km [1, 3, 4, 8, 9, 15]. Give one rider 3 neighbouring stops so that the stretch (last stop − first stop) is as short as possible.

The window size is fixed at 3; only its place is free. A window's stretch is its last stop minus its first, so after each slide you read only its two new ends: one subtraction, with no need to look at the middle.
[1, 3, 4] gives 3. Slide: 1 leaves and 8 enters, [3, 4, 8] gives 5. Then [4, 8, 9] gives 5 and [8, 9, 15] gives 7.
Best: stops 1, 3 and 4, a stretch of 3 km. One pass over the windows: O(n).
If two windows had tied, the question would have to say which one to return. Decide the tie rule before coding (here, the first one).

blocks.title: Imbalanced data: class weights, resampling and the right metric
blocks.builds_on: Day 17 · precision, recall and F1, Day 21 · ROC, AUC and picking the threshold, Day 8 · logistic regression and cross-entropy, and Day 10 · stratified splits and leakage
points: Imbalanced data: one class is rare, such as 1 fraud in 100 UPI payments. A model that always says "not fraud" is 99% accurate and catches nothing (Day 17), so accuracy lies here.

Measure the rare class: precision, recall and F1 (Day 17). ROC-AUC (Day 21) stays flattering when negatives are many, because false alarms barely move the false-positive rate. PR-AUC, the area under the precision–recall curve (scikit-learn's `average_precision_score`), shows them. A random model's PR-AUC is the share of positives, 0.01 here, not 0.5.
Stratify every split (Day 10), so each split keeps the same small share of positives. With 5% positives, an unlucky random split can leave a validation set with almost none.

Class weights make each mistake on the rare class cost more: cross-entropy (Day 8) multiplies each row's loss by its class's weight. `class_weight="balanced"` sets each class's weight to n ÷ (2 × its count), so at 1:99 one fraud row counts about 99 times a normal one.

Resampling: random oversampling copies rare rows; random undersampling drops common rows (fast, but it throws data away). Google's course downsamples, then upweights. Resample only the training split, after splitting: copies of one row on both sides of a split is Day 10's leakage, and validation must keep the real ratio.
Weights and resampling push the rare class's scores up, so at a 0.5 threshold recall rises and precision falls. They barely change the order of the scores, so ROC-AUC and PR-AUC stay about the same.
Often the simplest fix is moving the threshold (Day 21): keep the plain model and pick the threshold on validation, by cost or by F1.
Say which mistake costs more before you choose, and report precision and recall at the chosen threshold, not accuracy.
blocks.say: With rare positives I ignore accuracy and report precision, recall and PR-AUC on a stratified validation set, then fix the model with class weights, resampling of the training split only, or simply a better threshold.
example: 1,000 UPI payments in validation, 10 of them fraud. Never flagging anything gets 990 right: 99.0% accuracy, recall 0.
A model flags 30 payments and 8 are fraud: TP 8, FP 22, FN 2, TN 968. Accuracy (8 + 968) ÷ 1,000 = 97.6%, lower than doing nothing, yet it catches 8 frauds in 10: recall 0.8, precision 8 ÷ 30 ≈ 0.27.
Balanced weights for 10 fraud and 990 normal rows: fraud 1,000 ÷ (2 × 10) = 50, normal 1,000 ÷ (2 × 990) ≈ 0.505. One fraud row counts about 99 times a normal one in the loss.
Random scores give ROC-AUC 0.5 but PR-AUC only about 0.01, the fraud share. So a PR-AUC of 0.5 here is strong, while a ROC-AUC of 0.95 can still hide many false alarms.
Oversampling: split first, then copy the training split's fraud rows until they match its normal rows. Validation and test keep their real 1 in 100.

selftest.q: At 1 fraud in 100 payments, why is 99% accuracy no good, and what do you report instead?
selftest.a: Always saying "not fraud" scores 99% and catches nothing. Report precision, recall and F1 for the fraud class at a chosen threshold, and PR-AUC rather than ROC-AUC to compare models.

selftest.q: What does `class_weight="balanced"` do, and what happens to precision and recall at a 0.5 threshold?
selftest.a: It weights each class by n ÷ (2 × its count) in the loss, so mistakes on the rare class cost more. The rare class's scores rise, so recall goes up and precision down at 0.5; the order of the scores, and so the AUCs, barely change.

selftest.q: 2,000 payments, 20 of them fraud. A model flags 50 and catches 15. What are its accuracy, precision and recall?

blocks.title: Binary Search: finding a value, and where it would go
blocks.builds_on: Day 5 · binary search and recursion, and Day 1 · Big-O
points: Day 5 gave you two binary search loops. Today's new idea is why they are right: the invariant, one sentence about lo and hi that is true before every step. Say it first, and the start values, the loop condition and the updates follow from it.

Closed range, to find a value. Invariant: if the target is in the list, it is in nums[lo..hi], both ends included. So lo = 0 and hi = n − 1; loop while lo <= hi, because a range of one item still has to be checked; mid has been checked, so move to mid + 1 or mid − 1. When lo > hi the range is empty: not found.

Half-open, first-true. Invariant: everything before lo is false and everything from hi on is true. Start lo = 0 and hi = n (a pretend true just past the end). Loop while lo < hi; if mid is true, hi = mid (it may be the first); else lo = mid + 1. When lo == hi, that is the first true, or n if there is none.
Every step must shrink the range, or the loop never ends. When lo < hi, mid = (lo + hi) // 2 is below hi, so hi = mid shrinks it, and lo = mid + 1 always does.
Before submitting, check 0, 1 and 2 items by hand: an empty list, one item smaller, equal and larger than the target, and two items with the target at each place. Most off-by-one bugs show up there.

In Python, (lo + hi) // 2 can't overflow: integers grow as needed. In Java or C++ an int stops at about 2.1 billion, so lo + hi can wrap round to a negative number; there you write lo + (hi − lo) // 2. Say this in an interview.

binary-search: Binary Search: what should it return when the value isn't there? Say its Big-O.
search-insert-position: Search Insert Position asks where the target would go. Which of the two loops answers that, and what should it return when the target is bigger than every item?

blocks.say: I state the invariant first: for finding a value, the target is in nums[lo..hi], so I loop while lo <= hi; for "where would it go", everything before lo is false and from hi on is true, so I loop while lo < hi and land on the first true.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): departures in minutes, sorted: [5, 12, 12, 12, 30]. How many trains leave after minute 12? Find the first index whose value is > 12.
Invariant: everything before lo is ≤ 12, and everything from hi on is > 12. Start lo = 0, hi = 5: nothing is checked yet, so both parts are empty and it holds.
mid = 2: 12 > 12 is false, so index 2 and everything before it is ≤ 12: lo = 3. mid = 4: 30 > 12, so hi = 4. mid = 3: 12 > 12 is false, so lo = 4.
lo == hi == 4, the first index > 12. Trains after minute 12: 5 − 4 = 1. This is what `bisect.bisect_right(nums, 12)` returns.
Off-by-one checks: [] gives lo = hi = 0 (no trains), [12] gives 1 (no trains after it) and [30] gives 0 (one train). Three seconds each, and they catch a wrong start or a wrong update.

blocks.title: A 45-minute design framework: requirements to deep dives
blocks.builds_on: Day 4 · a request's journey, Day 11 · back-of-the-envelope estimates, Day 18 · API design, Day 25 · unique IDs, Day 27 · replication and choosing consistency per feature, and Day 28 · the 25-minute design question and its six items
points: A design interview runs about 45 minutes, and the order you work in matters as much as what you know: it shows you can drive the conversation. Day 28's question had no set order. This card's order is the primary's, plus two steps it leaves out: a quick estimate and a wrap-up.

Requirements, about 5 minutes. Functional: the three or so things users must be able to do, and what is out of scope. Non-functional, with numbers: how fast, how available, how much scale, and which features need consistency and which can be stale (Day 27). Speed is said as p99: "under 300 ms at p99" means 99 requests in every 100 finish within 300 ms, and only the slowest 1 in 100 may take longer.

Estimates, about 3 minutes (Day 11): only the numbers that change a decision, such as reads and writes per second, storage and the read-to-write ratio. The primary skips this step and does sums only when a choice needs one; this plan keeps a quick pass because its design questions score estimates.

Core entities, about 2 minutes: the main things the system stores, such as Show, Seat and Booking. Then the API, about 5 minutes (Day 18): the endpoints that cover the functional requirements, with methods, paths and status codes, and an idempotency key wherever a retry could double something.
High-level design, 10 to 15 minutes: boxes and arrows that make each API call work end to end, client to database (Day 4's journey). One requirement at a time, simplest version first.

Deep dives, about 10 minutes: go back to the non-functional numbers and fix what would break them, such as a cache, replicas or how IDs are made. The interviewer often picks; if not, pick the riskiest part.

A latency number from the requirements becomes a latency budget: split it across the hops of one request, where steps in a row add up and steps run side by side take the slowest. Today's guide lesson covers this part, so the reading below is shorter.
Wrap-up, 2 to 3 minutes (not in the primary): the bottlenecks, what you would watch in production, and what you would do with more time. Keep a clock: if requirements pass 8 minutes, move on.
blocks.say: I spend about 5 minutes on requirements with numbers, 3 on estimates that change decisions, 7 on core entities and the API, 10 to 15 on a simple end-to-end design, 10 on deep dives driven by the non-functional numbers, and close with bottlenecks.
example: A railway PNR-status page, first 15 minutes. Functional: look up a PNR's status; get a message when it changes. Out of scope: booking and payment.
Non-functional: a lookup in under 300 ms at p99; 10 million lookups a day; a status up to a minute old is fine (availability over consistency, Day 27).

Estimates: 10,000,000 ÷ 100,000 ≈ 100 lookups a second, and maybe 10 times that, 1,000 a second, when charts are prepared. 50 million live PNRs × 500 bytes = 25 GB: one database holds it, and reads far outnumber writes, so a cache earns its place.
Core entities: Pnr, Passenger and Subscription. API: GET /v1/pnr/{pnr} returns 200 with the status, or 404 for an unknown PNR. POST /v1/pnr/{pnr}/subscriptions with an Idempotency-Key returns 201.

Budget from the 300 ms: about 100 ms on the network, 20 ms for the load balancer and app server, 1 ms for a Redis hit or 20 ms for a database read on a miss. Worst case about 140 ms, leaving room for a retry and a bad day.
Then the high-level design (load balancer, stateless servers, cache-aside with a 60-second TTL, a database with followers), deep dives on the chart-time spike, and a wrap-up.

selftest.q: What is the invariant for the closed binary search loop, and why does it loop while lo <= hi?
selftest.a: If the target is in the list, it is in nums[lo..hi], both ends included. A range with one item (lo == hi) still has to be checked, so the loop runs until lo > hi, an empty range.

selftest.q: Why do Java and C++ programmers write lo + (hi − lo) / 2, and why doesn't Python need to?
selftest.a: lo + hi can pass an int's limit of about 2.1 billion and wrap round to a negative number. Python's integers grow as needed, so (lo + hi) // 2 is safe.

selftest.q: In [2, 4, 4, 4, 9], trace the first-true loop for "the first index whose value is > 4".
selftest.a: lo 0, hi 5. mid 2: 4 > 4 false, lo 3. mid 4: 9 > 4 true, hi 4. mid 3: 4 > 4 false, lo 4. lo == hi == 4.

selftest.q: Name the steps of the 45-minute design framework in order, with rough minutes.
selftest.a: Requirements, functional then non-functional with numbers (about 5); estimates (about 3); core entities and the API (about 7); high-level design (10–15); deep dives (about 10); wrap-up (2–3).

selftest.q: Positives are 2% of the rows. What PR-AUC and what ROC-AUC does a model with random scores get?
selftest.a: PR-AUC about 0.02, the share of positives. ROC-AUC 0.5. That is why a ROC-AUC that sounds high can hide many false alarms on rare positives.

first: Fridays start with revision. Today 5 minutes of this block go to a short guide lesson (listed in the CS block below), so the re-solves get about 5 minutes: enough for one Easy from the Revise row, not a medium from a blank file. Re-solve one if it fits and rate it; anything left shows again tomorrow. The rest of the block, about 20 minutes, is today's problem.
points: Today's new idea: lo and hi don't have to be indexes into a list. They can be the smallest and largest possible values, say 1 and n, and the "list" is never built.
Instead of reading nums[mid], you ask about mid with a call: an API that answers for one value, such as "higher, lower or correct" or "broken or fine".
Each call costs something, so count them: about log2(n). 1,000 values take at most 10 calls; 2^31, about 2.1 billion, take 31.
Day 32's loops work unchanged. A three-way answer (too low, too high, found) suits the closed loop, lo <= hi. A yes/no answer that flips once suits the first-true loop, lo < hi.
The invariant is still the guide: "the answer is in [lo, hi]". Each call rules out half of what is left.
Day 34 searches for the answer itself in the same way, and Day 36 writes its own check.

guess-number-higher-or-lower: Guess Number Higher or Lower is this idea in its plainest form. Read what its API returns before you pick a loop.

blocks.say: When the answer is a number in a known range, I binary search the values themselves, lo and hi as the smallest and largest possible, asking the check or API about mid, so it takes about log2(n) calls.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): builds 1 to 100 of an app; from some build on, every build is broken. `is_broken(v)` is the only way to look. Find the first broken build.
No list exists: lo = 1 and hi = 100 are values. The answer flips once from fine to broken, so use the first-true loop (Day 32).
The first broken build is 73. Calls: 50 fine (lo = 51), 75 broken (hi = 75), 63 fine (lo = 64), 69 fine (lo = 70), 72 fine (lo = 73), 74 broken (hi = 74), 73 broken (hi = 73).
lo == hi == 73 after 7 calls. log2(100) ≈ 6.6, so 7 is the most it can ever take; checking one build at a time could take 100.

blocks.title: Semaphores and producer–consumer with a bounded queue
blocks.builds_on: Day 26 · race conditions, mutexes and the with-lock block, Day 5 · threads share their process's memory, and Day 4 · a queue with deque
points: A mutex (Day 26) lets one thread in at a time. A semaphore is a counter of permits: `threading.Semaphore(3)` lets 3 threads in at once, and the fourth waits.

acquire takes a permit (the count goes down by 1) and waits if the count is 0; release gives it back and wakes one waiting thread. `with sem:` does both, even if an exception is raised. A semaphore of 1 works like a lock.
Use it to cap how many threads do something at once: at most 3 calls to a bank's API, or 10 open database connections.
Producer–consumer: producers put work into a shared buffer and consumers take it out, each at their own speed, like a kitchen putting dishes on a counter and delivery riders picking them up.

A bounded buffer holds at most N items. A full buffer makes producers wait and an empty one makes consumers wait. The producer waiting is back-pressure: a fast producer is slowed to the consumers' pace instead of filling memory.
Python's `queue.Queue(maxsize=N)` does all the locking for you: `put` blocks when it is full and `get` blocks when it is empty. OSTEP builds the same thing from semaphores.

To stop the consumers, the producer puts one sentinel (say `None`) per consumer after the last item; each consumer exits when it gets one. Across services the same idea becomes a message queue between programs, which Day 39 covers.
Time: about 15 minutes here for the reading and the kitchen task; the semaphore script is optional. The other 15 minutes of this block go to today's two guide lessons.
blocks.say: A semaphore is a counter of permits that caps how many threads run a section at once; for producer–consumer I use a bounded queue.Queue, so a full buffer blocks the producer (back-pressure), and one sentinel per consumer to stop them.
example: A payment app may make at most 3 calls to a bank at once: `sem = threading.Semaphore(3)`. Five threads, A to E, each run `with sem:` around their call.
A, B and C take permits and the count goes 3, 2, 1, 0. D and E find 0 and wait.
A finishes and releases, so the count is 1; D wakes and takes it, back to 0. There are never more than 3 calls in flight.

Kitchen and riders: `q = queue.Queue(maxsize=3)`. The kitchen puts orders 1 to 10; two riders each `get` one and take 0.05 s to deliver it. The counter fills to 3 almost at once, and the kitchen's next `put` waits until a rider takes one: the kitchen now runs at the riders' pace.
After order 10 the kitchen puts `None` twice, one per rider, and each rider stops when it gets `None`. With no maxsize the kitchen would finish at once and the orders would pile up in memory.

selftest.q: What is a semaphore, and how does it differ from a mutex?
selftest.a: A counter of permits: acquire takes one and waits at 0, release gives one back. A mutex lets one thread in; a semaphore of n lets n in at once.

selftest.q: In producer–consumer, what does a bounded buffer give you, and how does `queue.Queue(maxsize=3)` give it?
selftest.a: Back-pressure: once 3 items are waiting, `put` blocks, so a fast producer slows to the consumers' pace instead of piling items up in memory. `get` blocks when it is empty. The queue does its own locking.

selftest.q: How do the consumer threads know when to stop?
selftest.a: After the last item the producer puts one sentinel, such as `None`, per consumer; each consumer exits its loop when it gets one.

selftest.q: A yes/no API flips once somewhere in the values 1 to 1,000,000. At most how many calls does binary search need?
In the 45-minute design framework, what comes right after requirements, and why must non-functional requirements carry numbers?
selftest.a: A quick estimate, then core entities and the API. Numbers such as "under 300 ms at p99" or "4,000 reads a second" decide the design: they become a latency budget and say whether you need a cache or replicas.

blocks.title: Binary Search: whole-number square roots
blocks.builds_on: Days 32 and 33 · Binary Search, and Day 5 · binary search and recursion
points: Day 33 searched a range of values for a hidden number. Today the number you search for is the answer itself: the largest k for which a check holds.
The check is true for small k and false from some point on: true, true, true, false, false. You want the last true, the mirror image of Day 5's first true.
Way 1, with what you have: find the first k where the check is false (Day 5's first-true loop on the opposite check) and subtract 1, as Day 5's last_at_most did.

Way 2, a last-true loop: while lo < hi, mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2; if the check holds at mid, lo = mid, else hi = mid − 1. Invariant: lo is always a value known to pass (or the lowest possible answer), and everything above hi fails.
Why the + 1: when hi = lo + 1, (lo + hi) // 2 is lo. If the check holds there, lo = mid changes nothing and the loop never ends. Rounding up makes mid = hi, so the range always shrinks.
Before coding, say the lowest and highest possible answers, and check that the check really goes true-then-false with no flip back.

sqrtx: Sqrt(x) is this pattern in its plainest form. Write its check as one line before the loop. O(log x) checks.

blocks.say: When a check is true up to some value and false after it, I binary search for the last true, rounding mid up so the range always shrinks, or I find the first false and step back one.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): with 20 coins, how many full rows of a staircase can you build, where row n needs n coins? n rows need n(n + 1) ÷ 2 coins.
The check "n(n + 1) ÷ 2 ≤ 20" is true for 0 to 5 and false from 6: find the last true. lo = 0, hi = 20.
mid = (0 + 20 + 1) // 2 = 10: 55 coins, fails, hi = 9. mid = (0 + 9 + 1) // 2 = 5: 15 coins, passes, lo = 5.
Answer: 5 rows, using 15 coins with 5 left over, in 4 checks instead of trying up to 20.

blocks.builds_on: Days 29 and 30 · Sliding Window
first: Timer: 40 minutes. Stuck when it rings: one line in My notes on where, then take the help on its row one step at a time. Show the answer last and watch only the idea in its Video, then close it and code it from blank. Show the answer turns its bookmark on for you.
points: You solved Permutation in String and Minimum Size Subarray Sum (Day 30) with the variable window template (Day 29). This hard combines them: the shortest window whose letter counts cover a second string's counts.

minimum-window-with-characters: Step 1, brute force: write "the window covers t" as a rule about two count dicts. What must hold for every letter of t? Then say the cost of checking every substring that way.

Step 2, the template: grow right until the window covers t, then shrink from the left while it still covers, recording inside the shrink loop as for Day 30's shortest window. Comparing the counts at every step costs up to 52 letters (upper and lower case): O(52 × n).

Step 3, an O(1) check: Day 30's faster version kept a running number of letters whose counts already match. Here a letter of t is met when its count in the window reaches its count in t. At exactly which moment should that number go up as a letter enters, and down as one leaves?

A letter can be needed more than once (t = "aab"). Does a third a make that letter any more met than two did? And what should a letter that isn't in t do to your number? Test your Step 3 answer on both.

The answer is the substring, not its length, so decide what to store when you record. No covering window means "". Trace each step on paper first, on your own small example with one letter needed twice.

blocks.say: I grow the window until it covers every needed letter, shrink while it still covers to record the shortest, and keep the check O(1) with a running count of letters whose need is met.
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250): the weather by day is "rsrrcccs" (r rain, s sun, c cloud). Find the longest run of days with at most 2 kinds of weather. Keep counts, and kinds = how many kinds have a count of at least 1, so you never scan the dict.
Grow: r (kinds 1), s (2), r and r (still 2: more of a kind already there adds nothing). Days 0–3 are fine: record 4.
right = 4 adds c: kinds 3, too many. Shrink while kinds > 2: drop r (count 3 → 2, kinds stays 3), then drop s (count 0, kinds 2). left = 2, window 2–4.
right = 5 and 6 add c: window 2–6, record 5. right = 7 adds s: kinds 3. Drop r (count 1), drop r (count 0, kinds 2): left = 4, window 4–7, length 4.
Best 5, "rrccc" on days 2–6, recorded after each shrink. kinds changed only when a count went from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0, so each step was O(1).

blocks.title: Design a URL shortener: from your Day 28 answer to a full design
blocks.builds_on: Day 28 · your 25-minute design and its score on six items, Day 32 · the 45-minute framework, Day 25 · base62 codes from a counter, Day 13 · cache-aside, Day 20 · a unique key and indexes, Day 27 · followers and read-your-writes, Day 6 · stateless servers behind a load balancer, Day 18 · status codes, and Day 11 · estimates
points: Start from Day 28: your note has your 25-minute answer and its score on the six items (the journey and API, estimates, codes, the database, the cache, replicas). Today goes deeper on each, in Day 32's order, and spends longest on the ones you missed.

Requirements. Functional: shorten a long URL, redirect a short one, an optional custom alias and an optional expiry; accounts and editing are out of scope. Non-functional, with numbers: a redirect in under 100 ms at p99 on our side, redirects that keep working even when creating links doesn't, every code unique, and about 100 reads per write.

Estimates: 100 million new links a month is about 40 writes a second, so about 4,000 redirects a second on average and 12,000 at a 3× peak. Ten years is 12 billion links; at 500 bytes each, about 6 TB before copies. 6 base62 characters give 56.8 billion codes, so 7 leave plenty of room (Day 25).

Codes: a counter in base62 is unique by construction. Each server leases a block of, say, 1,000 numbers from one shared counter, so it asks once per 1,000 links. Counter codes are guessable; if that matters, mix the bits before encoding (scramble each number with a fixed formula that can be undone, so neighbouring numbers give unrelated-looking codes). A hash of the long URL cut to 7 characters needs no counter, but two URLs can get the same code, so insert with the code as a unique key and retry with a salt when it clashes.

Redirects: 301 (moved permanently) lets browsers cache it, so repeat clicks never reach you: less load, but no click counts and no way to change or expire the link. 302 (found) sends every click through you, so most shorteners pick it. Count clicks off the redirect's path: add 1 to the code's counter in Redis and copy the totals to the database every minute.

Reads: cache-aside in Redis for hot codes, since a few links get most clicks, with a TTL no longer than the link's expiry (Day 13). In the database the code is the primary key, so a lookup is one index read (Day 20). 6 TB fits a large PostgreSQL leader for a while; Day 41 splits it by code when it doesn't.

Replicas: redirects read from followers behind stateless servers (Days 6 and 27). A brand-new link may not have reached a follower yet, so put it in the cache when it is created, or read the creator's first clicks from the leader.

Aliases and expiry: a custom alias is one more insert against the same unique key, and a taken one gets 409 Conflict (Day 18). Make aliases at least 8 characters, so they can never equal a 7-character counter code. Store expires_at, check it on every read (404 once past) and delete expired rows in a nightly job.
blocks.say: I make codes from a counter in base62 with servers leasing blocks, store code → URL with the code as the primary key, serve redirects with a 302 from a Redis cache in front of read replicas, count clicks off the hot path, and handle aliases and expiry through the same unique key and an expires_at check.
example: Creating a link: server A has leased the block that starts at 62⁶ = 56,800,235,584, so every code has 7 characters. Its first link gets encode62(62⁶) = "1000000"; server B, on the next block, starts at "10000g8".

A inserts ("1000000", the long URL, expires_at) with the code as the primary key, puts it in Redis, and returns 201 with the short URL. No other server can hand out that number, so the insert never clashes.

Redirect: GET /1000000 → load balancer → any server → a Redis hit in about 1 ms → 302 with Location set to the long URL. On a miss it reads a follower in a few ms, fills the cache, then redirects. Either way it adds 1 to the code's click counter in Redis.
With 301 instead, a link clicked 1,000 times by 100 people reaches you about 100 times, once per browser, so your click count says 100. With 302 it says 1,000.
Hashing instead of a counter: with 7-character hashes, by the 12-billionth link a new code lands on a taken one about 1 time in 290, so the unique-key check and the retry are not optional.
A custom alias "diwali-sale" is inserted the same way; if the key exists, 409. A link whose expires_at has passed returns 404, and its cache entry never outlives it.

selftest.q: In a last-true binary search, why is mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2 and not (lo + hi) // 2?
selftest.a: When hi = lo + 1, rounding down gives mid = lo; if the check passes there, lo = mid doesn't move and the loop never ends. Rounding up makes mid = hi, so every step shrinks the range.

selftest.q: 301 or 302 for a URL shortener's redirect? Give the trade.
selftest.a: 301 is permanent, so browsers cache it: less load, but repeat clicks never reach you, so you lose click counts and can't change or expire the link. 302 sends every click through you, which is why most shorteners use it.

selftest.q: Short codes from a counter in base62, or from a hash of the long URL: what does each cost?
selftest.a: Counter: unique by construction with no clash checks, but it needs a shared counter (servers lease blocks) and the codes are guessable. Hash: no coordination and the same URL gets the same code, but codes can clash, so you need a unique-key check and a retry.

selftest.q: 100 million links a month, kept 10 years, at 500 bytes each: how many links, how much storage, and how many base62 characters?
selftest.a: 12 billion links and about 6 TB before replicas. 62⁶ ≈ 56.8 billion covers them, so 6 characters is the minimum; 7 (about 3.5 trillion) leaves room and makes hash clashes rarer.

selftest.q: 10 threads each hold a `Semaphore(3)` for 0.05 s. About how long do they take in all?
selftest.a: About 0.2 s: four rounds of 0.05 s, with 3, 3, 3 and then 1 thread inside.

blocks.title: Binary Search: searching a sorted matrix
blocks.builds_on: Days 32 to 34 · Binary Search, and Day 1 · Big-O
points: Some matrices have two rules: each row is sorted, and each row starts above where the row before it ended. Read row after row, such a matrix is one sorted list of rows × cols numbers.
What if you treat the matrix as that one list without building it? Copying it costs O(m × n), more than any search. Day 33 searched numbers that were never stored: what range would you search here?

Given a place in that pretend list, how do you find its row and column in the matrix? The worked example (the next step) shows the trick on cinema seats. Ask yourself whether you divide by the number of rows or of columns, and check it on a 2 × 3 grid.
The other way: binary search the rows first (the last row whose first number is ≤ the target), then search inside that row. Same Big-O, but two loops and twice the chances of an off-by-one.
Check the two rules before using the trick. If rows and columns are each sorted but a row can start below the previous row's end, the matrix is not one sorted list and this fails.

search-2d-matrix: Which of Day 32's loops fits, and what in it has to change? Say the Big-O before coding.
Edge cases: one row, one column, and a target below the first number or above the last.

blocks.say: When a grid's numbers can be read in order as one list, I binary search that list without building it, turning each position into a row and a column as I go.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): a cinema has 3 rows of 4 seats, numbered 0 to 11 row by row. Where is seat 7? divmod(7, 4) = (1, 3): row 1, column 3, both counted from 0.
The matrix [[1, 4, 9, 12], [15, 20, 25, 31], [40, 42, 50, 60]] follows both rules: read row after row it is 12 sorted numbers at positions 0 to 11.
Its median sits between positions 5 and 6. divmod(5, 4) = (1, 1) gives 20 and divmod(6, 4) = (1, 2) gives 25, so the median is 22.5, with no list built.

blocks.title: Sliding Window (hard): Sliding Window Maximum, and a new tool, the monotonic deque
blocks.builds_on: Day 26 · Sliding Window, Day 4 · queues and deques, and Day 7 · heaps
first: Today brings a new tool, the monotonic deque: a deque whose values only ever run one way from front to back, so its front is always the best item it holds. The worked example on its row (the step after the idea) builds one, for the cheapest price in each window of 3 days; work through it line by line before you code the fast version.

Timer: 40 minutes. Stuck when it rings: one line in My notes on where, then take the help on its row one step at a time. Show the answer last and watch only the idea in its Video, then close it and code it from blank. Show the answer turns its bookmark on for you.
points: You solved Contains Duplicate II (Day 26) with a fixed window, and Day 4's HitCounter task dropped old times off the front of a deque. This hard needs both, plus one new idea taught here: the monotonic deque.

sliding-window-maximum: Step 1, brute force: take the max of each window. Say its cost for n items and windows of k. Then ask why Day 26's running summary can't fix it: when the max leaves the window, what is the new max?
Step 2, a heap (Day 7) of (−value, index) gives the max at the top, but the top may have left the window. What can you do with a top whose index is too old? Say the cost.

The worked example (the next step) keeps the cheapest price; turn it round for the maximum. When a new item arrives, which items already in the deque can never be the max again while the new one is in the window? From which end do you pop them, so which way do the values run from front to back?

When does the front have to go, and why does that mean storing indexes rather than values? Then count how many times one index can be pushed and popped: that gives the cost of the whole pass, even with a loop inside a loop.
Step 3: code it with `collections.deque`. Trace on paper first, including the first k − 1 steps, which produce no answer yet.

blocks.say: I keep a monotonic deque of the items that could still be the answer, in order, so the front is always the window's answer and each index goes in and out at most once: O(n) for the whole pass.
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250): petrol prices by day [4, 2, 12, 3, 8, 5, 1]. Find the cheapest price in each window of 3 days. This is the mirror image: keep values increasing, and pop from the back any price larger than the new one.

Days 0–2: 4 goes in. 2 arrives: 4 can never be the cheapest again while 2 is in the window (2 is cheaper and leaves later), so pop 4. 12 goes in. Deque [2, 12] (indexes 1, 2). First window: the cheapest is the front, 2.
Day 3, price 3: pop 12 (larger), push 3. Deque [2, 3]. The front's index 1 is still inside the window 1–3: cheapest 2.
Day 4, price 8: push it, [2, 3, 8]. The window is now 2–4 and the front's index 1 has left, so pop it from the front: [3, 8], cheapest 3.
Day 5, price 5: pop 8, push 5: [3, 5], cheapest 3. Day 6, price 1: pop 5 and 3, push 1: [1], cheapest 1. Answer [2, 2, 3, 3, 1].
Each index was pushed once and popped at most once: O(n), against O(n × k) for scanning every window.

points: Day 0's LLD 5 asked for a parking lot's classes. Today you build one that runs, in 90 minutes, with Day 21's playbook: requirements, entities, services, a driver, slices that run, and a demo.

Requirements to agree first: levels of spots in three sizes (small, medium, large); bikes, cars and trucks; a vehicle fits a spot of its size or bigger; entry gives a ticket, exit returns a fee; a board shows the free spots of each size. Out of scope: payments and booking ahead.

Entities: Enums for VehicleType and SpotSize (Day 21); Vehicle(plate, type) and Ticket(id, plate, spot, entered_at) as dataclasses; Spot(id, size) knows whether it is free; Level holds spots. Service: ParkingLot, with park(vehicle, now) returning a Ticket and leave(ticket_id, now) returning the fee.
Strategy (Day 16) for the two rules that change: which free spot to give (smallest that fits, lowest level first) and how to charge (per started hour by vehicle type, or a flat day rate).
Factory (Day 23): `make_fee_policy(name)` turns the config's "hourly" or "flat" into a policy object, so callers never name the class.
Observer (Day 30): the display board subscribes to the lot, and after every park and leave the lot sends it the free count for each size. A second board at the exit is one more subscriber.
Pass the time in (now, in minutes), as on Day 25, so fee tests are exact. Raise clear exceptions (LotFull, UnknownTicket), and keep print and input in the driver.

Two gates parking at once could both grab the same free spot, a check-then-act race (Day 26). One lock around "find a free spot and take it" fixes it: say so in the demo, and build it only if time is left.
blocks.say: I agree the requirements, model vehicles, spots, levels and tickets as entities with enums for the fixed sets, put the parking rules in a ParkingLot service, make spot choice and fees Strategies built by a small factory from config, and let display boards subscribe as observers.
example: A smaller system through the same steps: a railway station's left-luggage lockers. Requirements: small and large lockers; a bag gets the smallest free locker that fits; a token on deposit; ₹30 for each started 24 hours on collection.

Entities: BagSize, an Enum of SMALL and LARGE; Locker(id, size, bag); Token(id, locker_id, deposited_at). Service: Cloakroom, with deposit(size, now) returning a Token and collect(token_id, now) returning the fee.
Strategies: SmallestFit.choose(lockers, size) gives a small bag a small locker before a large one; PerDayFee(30) works out the charge. Cloakroom receives both and never names their classes.
Observer: a Board subscribes; after each deposit and collect, Cloakroom calls on_change with the free count of each size.

Test with 2 small lockers and 1 large: three small bags fill both small lockers and then the large one, a fourth raises NoLockerFree, and a bag collected after 25 hours costs ₹60 (two started days). The parking lot is the same shape, with levels and three vehicle types.

blocks.title: Cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning
blocks.builds_on: Day 10 · train, validation and test sets, and leakage, Day 14 · bias and variance, Day 15 · λ, the regularisation strength you choose, Day 22 · random forests and max_depth, and Day 31 · stratifying when a class is rare
points: One validation split gives one noisy score: Day 22 noted that one row of 85 is more than a point. k-fold cross-validation reuses the training rows to get k scores instead of one.

k-fold: cut the training rows into k folds, often 5. Train on k − 1 of them and score the one left out, k times, so every row is scored exactly once. Report the mean and the spread (standard deviation) of the k scores.

Stratified k-fold keeps each class's share the same in every fold (Day 10's stratify, per fold). Use it for classification, above all with a rare class (Day 31). Shuffle first, unless the rows are in time order; then train on the past only (Day 10).

Hyperparameters are the settings you choose, not the weights the model learns: λ (Day 15), max_depth and the number of trees (Day 22). In scikit-learn's LogisticRegression, C is 1 ÷ λ, so a small C is a strong penalty.

Grid search tries every combination and keeps the best mean CV score: 5 values of C × 5 folds = 25 fits, plus one final refit on all the training rows. Random search tries a fixed number of random combinations, and with many settings it often finds as good a one faster.
The test set stays out of all of it: split it off first, cross-validate and tune on the rest, then score the test set once (Day 10). `GridSearchCV` does the folds, the search and the refit for you.

Anything that learns from data, such as StandardScaler, must be fitted inside each fold, or the fold's scored rows leak into the scaling. Put it in a `Pipeline` with the model, and every fold fits its own scaler.
Read the spread: if two settings' means differ by less than their spread, call it a tie and take the simpler one (Day 14).
blocks.say: I split off a test set, run stratified k-fold cross-validation on the rest with the preprocessing inside a Pipeline, pick hyperparameters by the mean CV score with grid or random search, and score the test set once at the end.
example: 10 training rows and k = 5, so folds of 2 rows. Round 1 trains on rows 2–9 and scores rows 0–1; round 2 trains on rows 0–1 and 4–9 and scores 2–3; and so on. Every row is scored exactly once.
Five fold accuracies: 0.90, 0.85, 0.95, 0.80 and 0.90. The mean is 0.88 and the standard deviation about 0.05, so a setting that scores 0.89 is not clearly better.
Grid search over C in [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100] with 5 folds: 25 fits, then 1 refit of the winner on all 10 rows, 26 in all.
With a Pipeline, each round's scaler learns its mean and spread from that round's 8 training rows only. Scaling all 10 first would let the 2 scored rows shape it (Day 10).
The test rows, split off before any of this, are scored once at the very end.

selftest.q: In the monotonic deque for a sliding-window maximum, why may you pop smaller values off the back when a new item arrives, and why is the whole pass O(n)?
selftest.a: The new item is bigger and leaves the window later, so the smaller ones can never be the maximum again while it is in the window. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so all the pops together are at most n.

selftest.q: Why does StandardScaler belong inside a Pipeline when you cross-validate?
selftest.a: So each fold fits its scaler on that fold's training rows only. Scaling all the rows first lets the scored rows shape the mean and spread, which is leakage (Day 10).

selftest.q: Two quick numbers: in a 3 × 4 matrix read row after row, where is position 9? And how many fits does a grid of 4 values of C with 5-fold cross-validation make, counting the final refit?
selftest.a: divmod(9, 4) = (2, 1): row 2, column 1. 4 × 5 = 20 fits, plus 1 refit = 21.

selftest.q: In the parking lot, which rules did you make Strategies, and what did the factory and the observer do?

selftest.q: Two ways to find the last k for which a true-then-false check holds?
selftest.a: A last-true loop with mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2, lo = mid on a pass and hi = mid − 1 on a fail; or the first-true loop on the opposite check, then subtract 1.

blocks.title: Binary Search: the slowest eating speed, and the smallest ship
blocks.builds_on: Days 32 to 35 · Binary Search, and Day 5 · binary search and recursion
points: Some problems ask for the smallest number that makes something possible: the slowest eating speed that still finishes in time, the smallest ship that carries everything in D days. The answer isn't in an array; it is a number somewhere in a range.

The key fact: the check "can it be done with s?" flips only once. If speed s is enough, every faster speed is enough too. So the checks for s = lo, lo + 1, … read no, no, no, yes, yes, and you want the first yes: Day 5's first-true loop, run over values like Day 33's guessing game.

Before any code, say the lowest and the highest possible answers out loud. Lowest: no smaller value could ever work. Highest: a value that surely works. A wrong bound is the most common bug here. For each of today's problems, also say what its check simulates and why it flips once.
Write the check as its own function, `can(s)`, returning True or False. It is usually one greedy pass that simulates the plan with s. Test it on two values by hand before you search.
Then the loop: `while lo < hi:` take mid; if `can(mid)`, hi = mid (mid might be the first yes); else lo = mid + 1. lo ends on the answer. Day 34 wanted the last yes; today wants the first.
Cost: the check is O(n) and runs about log₂(hi − lo) times, so O(n log range). For a range of 10⁹ that is only about 30 checks.
Edge cases: the answer equals lo or hi, one item, and very large numbers (fine in Python, whose integers don't overflow).

eating-bananas: Some checks round a division up: `(a + b - 1) // b`, or `math.ceil(a / b)`. Does this one?

blocks.say: When the question asks for the smallest value that makes something possible, I write a check that flips once from no to yes, set the lowest and highest possible answers, and binary search for the first yes in O(n log range).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): three delivery riders take 1, 2 and 3 minutes per delivery and work at the same time. What is the fewest minutes in which they can finish 5 deliveries between them?
The check: in t minutes the riders finish t // 1 + t // 2 + t // 3 deliveries. can(t) is True when that is at least 5. More minutes can only mean more deliveries, so it flips once.
Bounds: lo = 1 (nothing finishes in 0 minutes), hi = 5, since the fastest rider alone does 5 deliveries in 5 minutes.
mid = 3: 3 + 1 + 1 = 5, yes, so hi = 3. mid = 2: 2 + 1 + 0 = 3, no, so lo = 3. Now lo = hi = 3.
Answer 3 minutes. Two checks of O(n) each instead of trying every t: O(n log range).

blocks.title: Neural networks: neurons, layers and activations
blocks.builds_on: Day 8 · logistic regression, a weighted sum then the sigmoid, Day 3 · the weighted sum w1 × x1 + w2 × x2 + … + b, Day 7 · gradient descent, and Day 29 · vectors, dot products and E @ E.T
points: A neuron takes some inputs, computes a weighted sum plus a bias (Day 3), then passes it through an activation function. With the sigmoid as its activation, one neuron is exactly Day 8's logistic regression.
A layer is many neurons reading the same inputs. Put each neuron's weights in a column of a matrix W, and the whole layer is one matrix multiply: z = x @ W + b, then the activation on every number.

With a batch of examples as the rows of X (n × d), and W of shape d × h for h neurons, X @ W + b is n × h: every neuron's sum for every example at once, as Day 29's E @ E.T did every dot product at once.
ReLU is max(0, z): it keeps positive numbers and turns negatives into 0. It is cheap, and the usual choice for hidden layers. The sigmoid stays for a yes/no output.

Why an activation at all: without one, two layers are (X @ W1) @ W2 = X @ (W1 @ W2), a single linear layer, so depth adds nothing. The bend between layers is what lets a network learn curved boundaries.

A network is input → hidden layers → output layer, and the forward pass computes each layer from the one before. Write each step's shape as you go: a shape mismatch is the first thing to check when it breaks.

The output layer fits the task: one number for a price, one sigmoid for yes/no, and softmax for one of k classes. Softmax turns k scores into probabilities, e^(score i) ÷ the sum of e^(every score): all positive, adding up to 1, with the biggest score getting the biggest share.

Training is still Day 7's gradient descent, on every weight at once, with a loss such as Day 8's cross-entropy on the right class's probability. A network has thousands of weights, so Day 38 shows how to get all their slopes in one backward pass.
blocks.say: A layer is a matrix multiply plus a bias followed by an activation like ReLU; without the activation stacked layers collapse into one linear layer, and a softmax on the last layer turns the scores into class probabilities.
example: A tiny network: 2 inputs, a hidden layer of 2 ReLU neurons, and 3 output scores turned into probabilities by softmax. Input x = [1, 2].
Hidden neuron 1 has weights [0.5, 1.0] and neuron 2 has [−1.0, 0.25], biases 0. Sums: 0.5 × 1 + 1.0 × 2 = 2.5 and −1.0 × 1 + 0.25 × 2 = −0.5. After ReLU: [2.5, 0].
Hidden neuron 1's weights to the 3 outputs are [1.0, 0.2, −0.4]; neuron 2 output 0, so its weights add nothing here. Scores: 2.5 × [1.0, 0.2, −0.4] = [2.5, 0.5, −1.0].
Softmax: e^2.5 ≈ 12.18, e^0.5 ≈ 1.65 and e^−1 ≈ 0.37, total 14.20. Probabilities ≈ [0.858, 0.116, 0.026], adding up to 1.
In numpy, W1 is 2 × 2 (a column per hidden neuron) and W2 is 2 × 3. A batch of 32 inputs is a 32 × 2 matrix, and the output is 32 × 3: one row of probabilities per input.
Counting weights: a layer from d inputs to h neurons has d × h + h numbers, so a 784 → 128 → 10 network has 101,770 of them to train.

title: Rotated sorted arrays · State pattern

blocks.title: Binary Search: rotated sorted arrays
blocks.builds_on: Days 32 to 36 · Binary Search, and Day 5 · binary search and recursion
points: A rotated sorted array is a sorted list cut in two with the parts swapped: [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7] becomes [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]. It goes up, drops once, then goes up again.

The whole list isn't sorted, so "target smaller than mid, go left" no longer works. But cut it at any mid and at least one of the halves, lo..mid or mid..hi, is sorted, because the single drop can sit in only one of them.
To tell which, compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]. If nums[mid] < nums[hi], there is no drop between them, so mid..hi is sorted. Otherwise the drop is in mid..hi, so lo..mid is sorted.
Keep Day 32's habit: before coding, write in one line what is true of lo and hi at every step (for example, "if the answer exists, it is inside lo..hi"), and check each move keeps it true.

Today's two problems each ask a different question of the sorted half: one hunts for where the drop is, the other for a target. Say which question before coding, and trace it on a list rotated in the middle and on one not rotated at all.
Each step still drops half the range: O(log n) time, O(1) memory. Today's lists have distinct values; Day 38 adds duplicates, which break the comparison.
Edge cases: 1 and 2 items, and a list rotated all the way round (so it is simply sorted).

find-target-in-rotated-sorted-array: Once you know which half is sorted, what can its two ends tell you about whether the target is inside it? If it can't be there, where must it be? Test a target that is the first item after the drop.

blocks.say: In a rotated sorted array one half around mid is always sorted; I compare nums[mid] with nums[hi] to find that half, check from its two ends whether the answer can be in it, and drop the other half, so it stays O(log n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): the largest value in a rotated sorted list of distinct numbers, such as [50, 60, 70, 80, 10, 20, 30]. This time compare nums[mid] with nums[lo], the mirror of the nums[hi] test, and round mid up.

Invariant: the largest value is inside lo..hi. If nums[mid] > nums[lo], lo..mid rises with no drop, so the largest is at mid or after it: lo = mid. Otherwise the drop is inside lo..mid, so the largest sits before mid: hi = mid − 1.
lo = 0, hi = 6, mid = 3: 80 > 50, so lo..mid = [50, 60, 70, 80] is sorted and lo = 3.
lo = 3, hi = 6, mid = 5: 20 < 80, so the drop is inside 3..5 and hi = 4. lo = 3, hi = 4, mid = 4: 10 < 80, so hi = 3. lo = hi = 3: the answer is 80.
Check it on a list that isn't rotated, [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]: every mid is bigger than nums[lo], so lo walks right and ends on 50. One comparison per step picks the sorted half: O(log n).

blocks.title: State pattern: behaviour that changes with state
blocks.builds_on: Day 16 · Strategy, one small interface with a class per way, Day 21 · enums and illegal moves that raise, and Day 30 · Observer, telling subscribers when an order's status changes
points: Some objects behave differently depending on their state. A food order can be cancelled while it is placed or being prepared, but not once it is out for delivery. Written plainly, every method grows an `if self.status == …` chain, and a new state means editing all of them.

The State pattern gives each state its own class, and every state class has the same methods, one per event (prepare, pick_up, deliver, cancel). The object itself, the context, holds its current state object and passes each event to it.
Each state handles the event its own way and decides the next state: Placed.cancel moves the order to Cancelled; Delivered.cancel raises an error. Everything about one state lives in one class.
A handy shape: the base state class raises a clear error for every event, so each state overrides only the events it allows. An illegal event then fails loudly instead of silently doing nothing.

A transition table is the lighter option: a dict from (state, event) to the next state, with the states as an Enum (Day 21). Use it when states differ only in where they go next; use classes when they also behave differently, such as charging a cancellation fee in one state and not another.

State vs Strategy (Day 16): the same shape, an interface with a class per case. With Strategy the caller picks the object and it rarely changes; with State the states pick the next state themselves as events arrive.
Observer fits on top (Day 30): when the state changes, the context tells its subscribers, so the SMS and the restaurant's screen hear about it without the states knowing they exist.
Keep data that belongs to the order (its items, its attempts count) on the context, not in the state objects. Day 42 builds a vending machine with this pattern.
blocks.say: With the State pattern each state is a class that handles the same events and picks the next state, so the rules for one state sit together, illegal events fail loudly, and a new state is a new class instead of edits to every if-chain.
example: A food order goes Placed → Preparing → Out for delivery → Delivered, and can be Cancelled from the first two. Before: cancel(), prepare(), pick_up() and deliver() each have an if/elif on self.status.
After: an OrderState ABC with prepare(order), pick_up(order), deliver(order) and cancel(order), each raising IllegalTransition by default.

Placed: prepare → Preparing, cancel → Cancelled with a full refund. Preparing: pick_up → OutForDelivery, cancel → Cancelled with a ₹30 fee. OutForDelivery: deliver → Delivered. Delivered and Cancelled override nothing, so every event raises.
Order.cancel() is one line: `self.state = self.state.cancel(self)`. Adding a new Ready for pickup state between Preparing and Out for delivery is one new class plus a change to Preparing.
Test: place, prepare, pick up, then cancel raises IllegalTransition; a fresh order that is cancelled ends in Cancelled with no fee.

title: Duplicates, a time-based store · Backpropagation

blocks.title: Binary Search: rotated arrays with duplicates, and a time-based key-value store
blocks.builds_on: Day 37 · rotated sorted arrays, Days 32 to 36 · Binary Search, and Day 5 · binary search and recursion
points: Yesterday's test, comparing nums[mid] with nums[hi], assumed distinct values. With duplicates the two can be equal while the drop is on either side: [2, 2, 2, 0, 2] and [2, 0, 2, 2, 2] look the same at mid = 2 and hi = 4.

Second tool: Python's bisect module does Day 5's searches for you on a sorted list. `bisect_left(a, x)` is the first index with a[i] ≥ x; `bisect_right(a, x)` is the first index with a[i] > x. Both are O(log n).

From those two you get the usual questions: the first item ≥ x is `bisect_left`; the last item ≤ x is `bisect_right(a, x) - 1` (Day 5's last_at_most); and the count of items between lo and hi is `bisect_right(a, hi) - bisect_left(a, lo)`. Say which one a problem wants before you reach for a function.
For each of today's two problems, say before coding which of these ideas it needs, what you store, and what each operation costs.
Edge cases: a value smaller or larger than everything (bisect returns 0 or len(a)), a value equal to an item (left and right differ there), and a list where every value is the same.

search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii: When nums[mid] equals nums[hi] you can't tell which half is sorted. Can you still drop one item safely, so the range shrinks without losing any value? Look at what nums[hi] and nums[mid] have in common.

Whatever you do on a tie, can the worst case still be O(log n)? Think of a list where every value but one is the same: no method can beat O(n), because the one different value could be anywhere. Say this in the interview without being asked.
time-based-key-value-store: What do you keep per key, and does it stay sorted without `insort` (which costs O(n) per insert because items shift)? Which bisect call finds the latest timestamp ≤ t? Since Python 3.10, a `key=` argument lets bisect search a list of pairs by one field.

blocks.say: With duplicates, when nums[mid] equals nums[hi] I can't tell which half is sorted, so I shrink hi by one, which makes the worst case O(n); and on a sorted list I let bisect find the first item ≥ x or > x in O(log n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): the smallest value in a rotated sorted list that may contain duplicates, using Day 37's comparison of nums[mid] with nums[hi].

[2, 2, 2, 0, 2]: lo = 0, hi = 4, mid = 2. nums[mid] = 2 and nums[hi] = 2 are equal. [2, 0, 2, 2, 2] gives exactly the same picture at mid and hi, yet its drop is on the left, so equal values can't tell you the side.
Shrink: hi = 3. That is safe, because the 2 at hi has a copy at mid.
Carry on in the first list: mid = 1, nums[1] = 2 > nums[3] = 0, so the drop is to the right: lo = 2. mid = 2, 2 > 0 again: lo = 3. lo = hi = 3, and the minimum is 0.

The bisect idea on its own: delivery times [9, 11, 14, 14, 20]. How many fall between 11 and 14? bisect_right(a, 14) = 4 and bisect_left(a, 11) = 1, so 4 − 1 = 3 (11, 14, 14). The first time ≥ 12 is a[bisect_left(a, 12)] = a[2] = 14.

blocks.title: Backpropagation: the chain rule, step by step
blocks.builds_on: Day 7 · gradient descent and the MSE slopes, which it gave without showing where they come from, Day 36 · the forward pass through layers, and Day 8 · the sigmoid
points: Training needs the slope of the loss for every weight (Day 7). Day 7 handed you the MSE slopes as a formula. A network has thousands of weights, so you need a rule that finds all of them: the chain rule, applied backwards. That is backpropagation.
A slope (a derivative) answers: if I nudge this input a tiny bit, how much does the output move, per unit of nudge? y = 3x has slope 3: nudge x by 0.01 and y moves by 0.03.
The chain rule: when a change flows through a chain of steps, the slopes multiply. With y = 3x and z = 2y, nudging x by 0.01 moves y by 0.03 and z by 0.06, so dz/dx = 2 × 3 = 6.

Every step in a network is simple and has a known local slope. For z = w × x + b, the slope for w is x and for b is 1. The sigmoid's is p × (1 − p), where p = σ(z). A squared error (p − y)² has slope 2(p − y). ReLU's is 1 when z > 0 and 0 otherwise.

Backprop: run the forward pass and keep every value it computes. Then walk backwards from the loss, multiplying local slopes, to get each weight's slope. The backward pass reuses the forward pass's numbers, such as p in p × (1 − p).
If one value feeds several later steps, add up the slopes that come back along each path.

Why it is cheap: the slopes of all the weights in a layer share the same chain from the loss back to that layer. Walking backwards computes that shared part once, so the whole backward pass costs about as much as a forward pass or two, not one pass per weight.
Day 7's MSE slope, 2 × error × x, is this rule on the chain prediction → error → squared. You can always check a slope by nudging: (loss(w + h) − loss(w − h)) ÷ 2h, with h tiny, such as 0.00001.
blocks.say: Backpropagation is the chain rule applied backwards: I keep the forward pass's values, then multiply local slopes from the loss back to each weight, sharing the common part of the chain so all the gradients cost about one extra pass.
example: One neuron, one example: x = 2, w = 0.5, b = −0.5, true label y = 1, a sigmoid and a squared-error loss. Forward: z = 0.5 × 2 − 0.5 = 0.5, p = σ(0.5) = 0.6225, L = (p − 1)² = 0.1425. Keep z and p.
Local slopes, from the loss backwards: dL/dp = 2(p − y) = −0.7551. dp/dz = p(1 − p) = 0.2350, reusing p. dz/dw = x = 2, and dz/db = 1.
Chain them: dL/dw = −0.7551 × 0.2350 × 2 = −0.3549, and dL/db = −0.7551 × 0.2350 = −0.1774. The first two factors are shared, so compute them once.
Check by nudging: (L at w = 0.50001 − L at w = 0.49999) ÷ 0.00002 = −0.3549. The chain rule and the nudge agree.

Step with learning rate 1: w = 0.5 + 0.3549 = 0.8549 and b = −0.5 + 0.1774 = −0.3226, and the loss falls from 0.1425 to 0.0399. In a network the same walk carries on into the layer before, one more local slope at a time.

blocks.title: Linked List: reversing a list, and merging two sorted lists
blocks.builds_on: Day 4 · stack, queue and linked list, Day 22 · Two Pointers, and Day 5 · recursion and the base case
first: In Python, write `build(values)` → head and `to_list(head)` once, so your tests compare plain lists.
points: A linked list node holds a value and `next`. You can't jump to the i-th node; you hold a pointer and walk. Most linked-list problems are about changing `next` pointers without losing the rest of the list.

The one rule: before you overwrite `node.next`, save it (`nxt = node.next`); once it is overwritten, nothing else points to the rest of the list. So draw three or four boxes and their arrows first (Day 4), write the pointer moves in order, and check them on the drawing.
To build a new list, start with a dummy node and a tail pointer: append with `tail.next = node`, then `tail = node`, and return `dummy.next`. The first node needs no special case.

Recursion on a list: let the call handle the rest (`node.next`), then fix up this one node. The base case is None, or a single node. The call stack is n deep: O(n) memory, and Python stops near 1,000 calls (Day 5), so also know the loop version, which is O(1).
Edge cases: an empty list (head is None), one node, two nodes, and for two lists, one of them empty.

reverse-a-linked-list: Reverse Linked List is pure rewiring; write it both as a loop and recursively. The usual names are prev, cur and nxt.

example: Practice problem (not on today's list): remove every node with value 3 from 3 → 1 → 3 → 4.
The first node is a 3, so the head itself must go. Put a dummy in front, dummy → 3 → 1 → 3 → 4, with prev = dummy.
prev.next is 3: skip it with `prev.next = prev.next.next`. prev stays where it is, because its new next hasn't been checked yet. prev.next is 1: keep it, so prev = prev.next.
prev.next is 3: skip it. prev.next is 4: keep it. prev.next is None: stop. Return dummy.next: 1 → 4. Each change was one pointer, and the rest of the list was always reachable from prev.
Recursively: remove(None) is None. Otherwise rest = remove(node.next); if node is a 3, return rest; else set node.next = rest and return node. The base case is None, and the stack is n calls deep.

blocks.title: Message queues: async work, retries and at-least-once delivery
blocks.builds_on: Day 30 · Observer, which said that across services it becomes publish/subscribe through a message queue, Day 33 · producer–consumer with a bounded queue inside one program, Day 18 · idempotency keys, and Day 6 · stateless servers
points: A message queue is a service between programs: producers send messages to it, and consumers take them off and do the work later. It is Day 33's producer–consumer across machines, and it keeps messages safe through restarts. Kafka, RabbitMQ and Amazon SQS are common ones.

Why use one: async work (the order API replies "placed" at once, and the receipt email happens later), smoothing spikes (the queue absorbs a dinner-rush burst and workers drain it at their own pace), and decoupling (the producer doesn't know or wait for the consumers). The workers are stateless (Day 6), so you add more to go faster.

Queue vs topic: in a queue each message goes to one of the workers, which share the load. In a topic (publish/subscribe) every subscribing service gets its own copy: "order placed" reaches email, the restaurant's screen and analytics. That is Day 30's Observer across services.

Acks, in SQS-style queues: a consumer takes a message, does the work, then acknowledges it, and only then is it deleted. Until the ack it is only hidden; if no ack comes within the visibility timeout (say 30 seconds), it shows up again for another worker. Kafka, the primary's example, differs: messages stay in the log for a set time, and each consumer group commits an offset, how far it has read; a consumer that crashes before committing re-reads from the last commit.

So you get at-least-once delivery: a worker can finish the work and crash before its ack, and the message is processed twice. Make consumers idempotent: keep the ids of messages already handled (Day 18's idempotency key) and skip repeats.

A message that keeps failing, such as one with bad data, is retried a few times with growing waits, then moved to a dead-letter queue for a person to look at, so it doesn't block the rest. SQS-style queues have this built in; with Kafka you add retry and dead-letter topics yourself, as the primary shows. Today's guide lesson covers the retry waits (backoff with jitter).

Ordering: many workers on one queue don't keep order. Kafka keeps order within a partition, and messages with the same key (say an order id) always go to the same partition, so one order's events stay in order while different orders run side by side.
In an interview, say: what goes on the queue, queue or topic, at-least-once with idempotent consumers, retries and a dead-letter queue, and the key that keeps order.
blocks.say: I put slow or spiky work behind a message queue, use a topic when several services need the same event, accept at-least-once delivery by making consumers idempotent, send repeat failures to a dead-letter queue, and key messages by order id when order matters.
example: Rahul places an order. The order service saves it, publishes {"type": "order_placed", "order_id": "o42"} to the order-events topic and replies to the app in about 50 ms, without waiting for email or the restaurant.
Three subscriber groups each get their own copy: email, the restaurant's screen and analytics. Email runs 3 workers on one queue, so each email message reaches only one of them.

Email worker A takes o42, sends the email, records o42 as done, then crashes before its ack. After the 30-second visibility timeout, worker B gets o42, finds it in the done set, skips the email and acks.
A message with a broken order id fails 5 times, with longer waits between tries, then moves to the dead-letter queue. The messages behind it keep flowing.

Dinner rush: 2,000 orders a minute for 30 minutes, while the email workers manage 1,500 a minute. The queue grows to 15,000, then drains in 15 minutes once arrivals drop to 500 a minute. No order page waited for any of it.

blocks.title: Deadlock: the four conditions and how to prevent it
blocks.builds_on: Day 26 · mutexes and the with-lock block, whose last point promised this day, Day 33 · semaphores and producer–consumer, and Day 12 · starvation and aging
points: Deadlock: two or more threads each wait for something another one holds, so none of them can ever move. Day 26's case: thread 1 holds lock A and waits for B, while thread 2 holds B and waits for A.

It needs four conditions at once: mutual exclusion (a lock has one owner at a time), hold and wait (a thread keeps what it holds while it waits for more), no preemption (nobody can take a lock away from its owner), and circular wait (a ring of threads, each waiting for the next).
Break any one and deadlock can't happen. The usual fix is lock ordering: every thread takes locks in one agreed order, say by account id, so no ring can form.

Backing off also works: `lock.acquire(timeout=1)` returns False instead of waiting for ever, so you release the lock you already hold, wait a moment and retry. OSTEP files this under no preemption: the thread takes its own lock away. Using one lock instead of two also works, at the cost of less work running in parallel.
Day 33's tools can deadlock too: a producer waiting for space in a full buffer while holding a lock the consumer needs before it can take anything out.

Livelock: threads keep reacting to each other, say both backing off and retrying in step, and none makes progress; a random wait breaks the rhythm. Starvation: one thread never gets its turn while others do, like Day 12's low-priority job.
blocks.say: Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait all at once, so I break one, usually circular wait by taking locks in a fixed global order, or no preemption by acquiring with a timeout and releasing what I hold.
example: Transfers between two accounts: transfer(x, y) takes x's lock, then y's. Thread 1 runs transfer(A, B) while thread 2 runs transfer(B, A).
Thread 1 takes A's lock and thread 2 takes B's. Thread 1 asks for B and waits; thread 2 asks for A and waits. All four conditions hold: deadlock.
Fix with ordering: always lock the account with the lower id first. Both threads now ask for A first; one gets it and the other waits holding nothing, so there is no ring.

Fix with a timeout: if `second.acquire(timeout=1)` returns False, release the first lock, sleep a random few milliseconds and retry. Without the random sleep, both threads can retry in step for ever: a livelock.

blocks.title: Sharding: partition keys, hot spots and consistent hashing
blocks.builds_on: Day 27 · replication, which copies the data, Day 20 · PostgreSQL, indexes and transactions, Day 11 · estimates that show when one machine isn't enough, and Day 34 · the URL shortener, looked up by its code
points: Replication (Day 27) copies all the data to each machine: it spreads reads and survives failures, but every machine still holds everything and takes every write. Sharding (partitioning) splits the data: each shard holds part of the rows, so storage and writes spread too. Shard when the estimates (Day 11) say one machine can't hold the data or take the writes.

The partition key is the column that decides a row's shard: user_id, restaurant_id, the short code. Choose it so the hot queries touch one shard: with user_id as the key, "this user's orders" is one shard's lookup.

Range sharding: keys a–f on shard 1, g–m on shard 2, and so on. Range queries stay cheap, but hot ranges (today's dates, the newest ids) pile onto one shard. Hash sharding: shard = hash(key) % n spreads keys evenly, but a range query must ask every shard, and changing n moves almost every key.

Consistent hashing: put machines and keys on a ring of hash values; a key belongs to the first machine clockwise from it. Adding a machine takes keys only from the one next to it, so about 1/n of the keys move instead of almost all.
Virtual nodes: put each machine at many points on the ring, say 100. The load evens out, and a new machine takes a little from every other machine instead of a lot from one.

Hot keys: one celebrity, or one huge restaurant chain on a festival day, gets far more traffic than the rest, and hashing can't split a single key. Cache it (Day 13), split it into key#1 … key#10 and combine on read, or give it a shard of its own.

The costs: a query that doesn't include the key must ask every shard and merge the answers, joins across shards are slow, and a transaction across shards is hard (Day 46). Resharding moves data while the system runs: copy, write to both, then switch.

Sharding plus replication: each shard has its own leader and followers (Day 27), so 5 shards × 3 copies is 15 machines. Say both: "shard by X for writes and size, replicate each shard for reads and failover."
blocks.say: I shard when one machine can't hold the data or the writes, pick a partition key that keeps the hot queries on one shard, place keys with consistent hashing and virtual nodes so adding a machine moves only about 1/n of them, handle hot keys separately, and replicate every shard.
example: The URL shortener from Day 34 outgrows one machine. Redirects look up one code, so shard by the code: each redirect touches one shard.
With hash(code) % 4 and 4 shards, add a fifth: a key stays put only if hash % 4 equals hash % 5. In a run with 100,000 keys, 80% of them moved.

A ring instead: hash each machine's name to a point on 0 … 2³² and each key to a point too; a key goes to the first machine clockwise. A new machine E takes only the keys between its point and the machine before it.

With 100 virtual nodes per machine, adding E moved about 15% of the keys, a little under the ideal 20%, because 100 points still leave some unevenness; every one of them went onto E. With one point per machine, the four machines' shares before adding E ranged from 10% to 31%.
Each shard then gets a leader and two followers (Day 27): 5 shards × 3 copies = 15 machines, with each shard failing over on its own.

Step 2, a cut: split A into A[:i] and A[i:], and B into B[:j] and B[j:]. If the two left parts together must hold half of all the items, what is j once you choose i? Then write down what must be true of the four numbers beside the two cuts for every left item to be ≤ every right item.

Step 3: when a cut breaks that rule, which way must i move, and why? Binary search i over 0 … m in the shorter list (why the shorter one?). Once the rule holds, where does the median come from? Say the cost.
A cut at the very start or end of a list has nothing on one side: use `float('-inf')` and `float('inf')` for the missing neighbours, so the comparisons need no special cases.
Trace on paper first: A = [1, 3, 8], B = [2, 4, 5, 9] (median 4), and A = [1, 2], B = [3, 4] (median 2.5). Cut each by hand before coding.

blocks.say: I first merge until the middle in O(m + n), then binary search a cut in the shorter list so the two left parts hold half the items and every left item is at most every right item, which gives the median in O(log min(m, n)).
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250): A = [1, 4, 7, 10] and B = [2, 3, 9, 12] are sorted. Someone cuts each list into a left and a right part. Check, without merging, whether every left item is ≤ every right item.

Inside one list nothing needs checking: it is sorted, so its left part is already ≤ its right part. Only the two cross pairs matter: A's last left item against B's first right item, and B's last left item against A's first right item. Two comparisons, O(1).
Cut A after 2 ([1, 4] | [7, 10]) and B after 2 ([2, 3] | [9, 12]): 4 ≤ 9 and 3 ≤ 7, so both hold and every left item is ≤ every right item.
Cut A after 3 ([1, 4, 7] | [10]) and B after 1 ([2] | [3, 9, 12]): 2 ≤ 10 holds, but 7 ≤ 3 fails. A left item, 7, is bigger than a right item, 3, so this pair of cuts is wrong.

blocks.title: Machine coding: build a vending machine with the State pattern
blocks.builds_on: Day 37 · the State pattern, Day 21 · the machine-coding playbook and enums, Day 16 · Strategy, Day 35 · the parking lot, the last machine-coding round, and Day 5 · recursion and its base case
points: A 90-minute machine-coding round, like Day 21's playbook and Day 35's parking lot: 10 minutes for requirements, entities and states, then build in slices that run, then tests and a demo.

Requirements: accept ₹1, ₹2, ₹5 and ₹10 coins; slots (A1, B2, …) each hold a product with a price and a count; select a slot; dispense and give change; cancel for a refund; clear errors for a sold-out slot, not enough money, and change the machine can't make.

Entities: Coin, an Enum whose value is its rupees (Day 21); Product(name, price); an Inventory from slot to product and count; and a coin box, a Counter of the coins the machine holds. Keep money in whole rupees, never floats.

The machine is Day 37's State pattern: Idle (no money in) and HasMoney (a balance). Both handle insert, select and cancel: Idle.select says "insert money first"; HasMoney.select makes the sale. Add a state only when the behaviour differs.

Make a sale in a safe order: check the slot isn't sold out, then that the balance covers the price, then that the change can be made from the coin box, and only then dispense, lower the count and pay out. A failed check changes nothing, like Day 20's all-or-nothing transaction.

Change-making is a Strategy (Day 16). Largest coin first works when every coin is plentiful, but the machine holds only so many: ₹6 from one ₹5 and three ₹2s gets stuck after the ₹5, while three ₹2s work. An exact strategy tries fewer of the big coin when it gets stuck: a small recursion (Day 5), new here and optional today.
Keep print and input in a driver (Day 21), so tests can script whole sales. Leave 10 minutes to demo a sale with change, a refund and a sold-out slot.
Extensions to discuss: notes and UPI as other ways to pay, an admin restock mode, and a display that subscribes to state changes (Day 30).
blocks.say: I model the vending machine as states that each handle insert, select and cancel, keep coins as an enum and money in whole rupees, check stock, balance and change before dispensing anything, and plug change-making in as a strategy.
example: Stock: A1 is Chips at ₹20, 2 left; B2 is Biscuits at ₹15. The coin box holds three ₹5s and three ₹2s. State: Idle.

Insert ₹10, ₹10 and ₹5: the state is HasMoney with a balance of ₹25. select("A1"): in stock, 25 ≥ 20, and ₹5 of change is one ₹5 from the box. Dispense Chips, A1 drops to 1, return [₹5], back to Idle.
Insert ₹10, then select("B2"): 10 < 15, so the machine says "insert ₹5 more" and stays in HasMoney with ₹10.
cancel(): refund the ₹10 coin, balance 0, back to Idle.
Each event went to the current state object; the machine itself only held the stock, the coins and the state.
