blocks.title: Training loops: mini-batches, learning rate, momentum and Adam
blocks.builds_on: Day 7 · gradient descent, epochs and a first mention of mini-batches, Day 38 · backpropagation gives every weight's slope, Day 14 · training vs validation error, and Day 15 · early stopping
points: A training loop: for each epoch, shuffle the data and cut it into mini-batches; for each batch, run the forward pass, the loss, the backward pass (Day 38) and an update of every weight. After each epoch, compute the validation loss.

Batch size: all the data per step (batch gradient descent: smooth but slow steps), one example per step (stochastic: cheap but noisy), or a mini-batch of 32 to 512 (the usual: GPUs run a batch in parallel, and a little noise helps escape flat spots). Steps per epoch = examples ÷ batch size.
Learning rate (Day 7): too big and the loss jumps around or blows up; too small and it crawls. Try 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 and watch the curve. It is often lowered as training goes on.
Momentum: keep a running average of recent gradients, m = 0.9 × m + 0.1 × g, and step along m. Directions that agree build up speed, and zig-zags cancel out, like a ball rolling downhill.

Adam adds a step size per weight to momentum. Besides m, the running average of gradients, it keeps v, the running average of squared gradients, and steps by lr × m ÷ (√v + ε). A weight with big, noisy gradients takes smaller steps; one with small gradients takes relatively bigger ones.

m and v start at 0, so for the first steps they are too small. Adam divides them by (1 − β₁ᵗ) and (1 − β₂ᵗ) at step t (the bias correction). The defaults lr = 0.001, β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999 and ε = 10⁻⁸ make it the usual first choice.

Reading loss curves (Day 14): both falling, keep going; training falling while validation turns up, overfitting, so stop and keep the best epoch (Day 15's early stopping); both flat and high, underfitting or too small a learning rate; jumping or NaN, too big a learning rate.
blocks.say: I train in mini-batches, tune the learning rate by watching the training and validation curves, and default to Adam, which is momentum plus a per-weight step size from the running average of squared gradients, with early stopping on validation loss.
example: 50,000 food orders with a batch size of 100: 500 steps per epoch, so 10 epochs are 5,000 weight updates.
Momentum with m = 0.9m + 0.1g: gradients 4, −4, 4, −4 give m = 0.4, −0.04, 0.36, −0.07, so the zig-zag cancels. Gradients 4, 4, 4, 4 give 0.4, 0.76, 1.08, 1.38, building speed.

Adam's first step for two weights, one with gradient 4 and one with 0.01: m = 0.1g and v = 0.001g², and after the correction m̂ = g and v̂ = g². Both steps are 0.001 × g ÷ |g| = 0.001: the same size, however different the gradients.
Without the correction the first step would be 0.001 × 0.1g ÷ √(0.001g²) ≈ 0.0032, three times too big. The correction keeps the first steps the right size.
Curves: from epoch 1 to 5 training loss falls from 0.9 to 0.3 and validation from 0.95 to 0.40. Then training keeps falling to 0.1 while validation climbs to 0.55. Stop and keep epoch 5's weights.

selftest.q: What does Adam add to momentum?
selftest.a: A step size per weight: it also keeps a running average of squared gradients, v, and divides each step by √v. It also corrects m and v for starting at 0, so the first steps are the right size.

selftest.q: With lr = 0.001, how big is Adam's first step for a weight with gradient 4, and for one with gradient 0.01?
selftest.a: Both 0.001. After the correction m̂ = g and v̂ = g², so the step is 0.001 × g ÷ |g|, whatever the gradient's size.

selftest.q: In the vending machine, why check the change before dispensing?
selftest.a: So the machine never takes the money, dispenses, and then finds it can't pay the change. If the change can't be made, nothing changes and the customer is told, like an all-or-nothing transaction.

selftest.q: Median of Two Sorted Arrays: what is the simple O(m + n) way, and what does the faster way binary search?
selftest.a: Simple: walk both lists with one pointer each until the middle. Faster: binary search the cut in the shorter list so the two left parts hold half the items and every left item is ≤ every right item: O(log min(m, n)).

selftest.q: Day 41: why does hash % n move most keys when a machine is added, and roughly how many move with consistent hashing?
selftest.a: A key keeps its shard only if hash % n equals hash % (n + 1), which is rare, so about n/(n + 1) of the keys move: 80% going from 4 to 5. With consistent hashing only about 1/(n + 1) move, all to the new machine.

blocks.title: Linked List: copying a list with extra pointers, and adding two numbers
blocks.builds_on: Days 39 to 42 · Linked List, and Day 22 · Two Pointers
points: Two ideas today: copying a list whose nodes point to more than their next node, and building a new list while walking two old ones at once.

copy-linked-list-with-random-pointer: A deep copy makes new nodes, and every pointer in the copy must point to new nodes, never back into the old list. A pointer to any node in the list is the hard part: the node it points to may not have been copied yet.
A dict from old node to new node solves it. When can you fill it, and when can you use it to set the copy's pointers? O(n) time and O(n) extra memory.
Nodes can be dict keys: a plain class is hashed by identity, so two nodes with the same value stay different keys. A `@dataclass` node is not hashable by default, so use a plain class.
Draw three nodes and their extra pointers first, one of them pointing to itself, and decide what the lookup does with None.
add-two-numbers: Walking two lists at once: keep one pointer in each (Day 22) and move both every step. The new part is deciding what happens when one list ends before the other.

Add Two Numbers stores the digits ones first, the order you add them on paper. Before coding, answer: when one list runs out first, what do you add for it? When exactly may the loop stop? Where would a dummy head (Day 39) save you a special case?
Edge cases to test: lists of different lengths, 99 + 1, and a single node.

blocks.say: To deep-copy a list with extra pointers I map each old node to its copy in one pass and wire the pointers through that dict in a second; to combine two lists I walk both at once behind a dummy head, carrying what overflows.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): deep-copy 3 orders, each with an item and a customer. Two of them point to the same Customer object: o1 (book, Asha), o2 (pen, Ravi), o3 (lamp, Asha). The copy must share customers the same way: 3 new orders and exactly 2 new customers.
Copying each order's customer on its own gives 3 new customers: the copy of o3 gets a second, separate Asha, so a change to Asha in the copy would miss one of her orders.
Keep copies = {} from old customer to new. For each order, if its customer isn't in copies yet, make a new customer and store it there; then point the new order at copies[old customer].
o1: Asha isn't in copies, so create a new Asha. o2: Ravi isn't either, so create a new Ravi. o3: Asha is already there, so reuse the new Asha.
Check: 3 new orders, len(copies) == 2, the copies of o1 and o3 point to the same new Asha (`is` gives True), and no copy points to an old customer. One pass over n orders: O(n) time and O(n) memory.

blocks.title: Making training work: initialisation, batch norm, dropout
blocks.builds_on: Day 38 · the backward pass multiplies local slopes along the chain, Day 36 · a layer is a matrix multiply plus a bias, then ReLU, Day 10 · standardising features with a mean and a spread, Day 15 · regularisation against overfitting, and Day 42 · mini-batches
points: A deep network can fail to train even with the right loss and optimiser. Three tools fix the usual causes: careful starting weights, batch norm and dropout.

Vanishing and exploding gradients: backprop multiplies one local slope per layer (Day 38). If those factors are mostly below 1, the gradient shrinks layer after layer and the early layers barely learn; mostly above 1, it blows up and the loss jumps to nan. Ten factors of 0.5 give about 0.001; ten factors of 2 give 1,024.

Initialisation: all-zero weights make every unit in a layer compute the same thing and get the same update, so they never become different. Start small and random, scaled to the number of inputs n: Xavier uses a spread of about √(1/n) for sigmoid-like activations, and He uses √(2/n) for ReLU, so each layer's outputs stay about as spread out as its inputs.

Batch norm: for each unit, take its outputs over the mini-batch, subtract their mean and divide by their standard deviation (plus a tiny ε, so you never divide by 0). It is Day 10's standardising, done inside the network. Then it multiplies by a learnt scale γ and adds a learnt shift β, so the layer can still choose its own range.

In training, batch norm uses the current mini-batch's mean and spread and keeps a running average of them. At prediction time it uses the running averages, because one input on its own has no batch. It lets you use larger learning rates and makes training less sensitive to the starting weights.

Dropout: in training, switch each unit off with probability p (say 0.5) by multiplying it by 0, and scale the survivors by 1 ÷ (1 − p) so the expected total stays the same. No unit can rely on one particular partner, which works as regularisation (Day 15).
Both behave differently in training and prediction. In PyTorch you switch with `model.train()` and `model.eval()`; in your own code, pass a `training` flag. At prediction time dropout does nothing.

Reading the symptoms: a loss that turns to nan points to exploding values (lower the learning rate, check the starting weights); a training loss stuck flat from the start points to vanishing gradients or dead ReLU units; a low training loss with a much higher validation loss calls for more dropout or other regularisation.
blocks.say: Gradients multiply layer by layer, so I start the weights at He or Xavier scale, add batch norm to keep each layer's outputs standardised over the mini-batch, and use dropout in training only, switching both to their prediction behaviour with eval().
example: One unit's outputs over a mini-batch of 4: [2, 4, 6, 8]. The mean is 5; the variance is (9 + 1 + 1 + 9) ÷ 4 = 5, so the standard deviation is √5 ≈ 2.24.
Standardise with (x − 5) ÷ 2.24: [−1.34, −0.45, 0.45, 1.34], with mean 0 and spread 1.
Scale and shift with the learnt γ = 2 and β = 1: [−1.68, 0.11, 1.89, 3.68]. Training updates γ and β like any other weight.
Dropout with p = 0.5 on outputs [3, 1, 4, 2]: the random mask [1, 0, 0, 1] keeps the first and the last, and scaling by 1 ÷ (1 − 0.5) = 2 gives [6, 0, 0, 4].
At prediction time dropout passes [3, 1, 4, 2] through unchanged. In training, each output's expected value is still its input: half the time 0, half the time double.

selftest.q: Why do deep networks suffer from vanishing or exploding gradients?
selftest.a: Backprop multiplies one local slope per layer. Factors mostly below 1 shrink the gradient towards 0 over many layers, so early layers barely learn; factors mostly above 1 make it blow up.

selftest.q: What does batch norm do to one unit's outputs, and why does it then apply γ and β?

selftest.q: Dropout with p = 0.25 on outputs [4, 8, 2, 6], and the mask keeps the 1st, 2nd and 4th. What comes out in training, and at prediction time?

selftest.q: Copying a list with random pointers: why two passes with a dict, not one?

selftest.q: What does momentum keep, and what does Adam add to it?
selftest.a: Momentum keeps a running average of the gradients and steps along it. Adam adds a per-weight step size, scaled down for weights whose gradients have been large.

title: A duplicate number, reversing part of a list · Singleton and dependency injection

blocks.title: Linked List: finding a duplicate number, and reversing part of a list
blocks.builds_on: Days 39 to 43 · Linked List, and Day 4 · nodes and next pointers
points: Two ideas today: finding where a loop starts, the second phase of Day 40's fast and slow pointers, and reversing only part of a list.

Day 40's pointers meet somewhere inside the loop, not necessarily at its start. Phase 2: put one pointer back at the head, leave the other at the meeting point, and move both one step at a time. Where they meet is the loop's entrance. Check it on a loop whose entrance is the head itself.

Why it works: when they first meet, fast has walked twice as far as slow, and the extra distance is a whole number of laps. So walking the tail's length from the meeting point lands on the entrance, the same place you reach by walking the tail from the head. In an interview, "the extra distance is whole laps" is enough.

find-duplicate-integer: Find the Duplicate Number forbids changing the array and wants O(1) extra memory. Every value is a valid index, so ask: what if you read nums[i] as "the node after i"? What would two equal values look like in that picture, and which of today's ideas finds it?
reverse-linked-list-ii: Reversing only positions left to right: reverse the stretch with Day 39's loop, which saves next before changing it, then work out on paper which two pointers must be reconnected at its two ends.
When left is 1 there is no node before the stretch. What from Day 4 gives it one, so it needs no special case?
Before coding, draw the four nodes that matter (the one before the stretch, its first, its last and the one after) and count how many pointers change.
Edge cases: left equal to right (nothing changes), and a stretch that is the whole list.

blocks.say: To find where a loop starts I let fast and slow pointers meet, then restart one from the head and step both by one until they meet at the entrance; an array of indexes is just a list of next pointers.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): a bus route where each stop names the next one: A → B → C → D → E → F → G, and G → D again. Where does the loop start?
Phase 1, slow one stop and fast two: (B, C), (C, E), (D, G), (E, E). They meet at E after 4 steps, inside the loop but not at its start.
Phase 2: slow goes back to A, fast stays at E, and both move one stop at a time: (B, F), (C, G), (D, D). They meet at D, the entrance.
Check: the tail A → B → C → D is 3 stops, and E is also 3 stops before D going round the loop (E → F → G → D). That is why the same number of steps works from both places.
O(n) time and O(1) memory. A set of visited stops finds D too, but with O(n) memory.

blocks.title: Singleton, and why passing dependencies in is better
blocks.builds_on: Day 14 · dependency inversion, passing objects in from outside, Day 9 · one reason to change, Day 26 · locks and check-then-act races, and Day 23 · one place that creates objects
points: Singleton: a class that allows only one instance and gives everyone a global way to reach it, such as `AppConfig.instance()`. It is meant for things that must exist once: one config, one connection pool.

The classic version keeps the instance in a class attribute and creates it on the first call. With threads, that first call is Day 26's check-then-act: two threads can both see "no instance yet" and make two. Guard the check and the creation with one lock.
In Python the usual singleton is simpler: create one object at module level (`config = load_config()` in config.py). A module is imported once, so every `import` gets the same object.

Why reviewers push back: any code can reach the instance, so it is hidden global state. A method's signature no longer shows what it uses, one test's changes leak into the next, and you can't swap in a fake without patching.
It also breaks Day 9's single responsibility: the class does its job and also controls how many of it exist.

Dependency injection: a class receives what it uses through its constructor, `OrderService(repo, sms)`, instead of fetching a global (Day 14). The signature shows its dependencies, and a test passes a fake.
When one shared instance is right, create it once at start-up in main() and pass the same object to everyone who needs it. You keep "only one" without the global access.
In an interview: "I'd create one instance at start-up and inject it, rather than a Singleton, unless a framework forces one."
blocks.say: A Singleton guarantees one instance but adds hidden global state that makes testing painful, so I create the one shared object at start-up and pass it in through constructors, which keeps it single and swappable.
example: A food app's OrderService sends an SMS when an order is placed. Singleton style: inside place(), it calls `SmsGateway.instance().send(phone, text)`.
To test place(), you can't stop a real SMS going out without patching SmsGateway, and nothing in OrderService's signature says it sends SMS at all.
Injected: `OrderService(sms)` stores the gateway, and place() calls `self.sms.send(phone, text)`.
main() builds one `SmsGateway(api_key)` and passes the same object to OrderService and RefundService: still one instance, created once.
The test passes a FakeSms that appends each message to a list, then asserts the list holds one message for the customer's phone.

blocks.builds_on: Days 39 to 44 · Linked List, Day 4 · queues, Day 13 · caching, and Day 33 · producer–consumer
points: Two design problems today: you write a class whose every method is O(1).

design-circular-queue: A circular queue keeps a fixed list of size k and never shifts items (shifting is what makes Day 1's pop(0) O(n)). If you keep the index of the front item (head) and how many items it holds (count), where is the next free slot, and how do positions wrap round to 0? Check it with k = 4, head = 3 and count = 2: slot 1.
With a count, full is count == k and empty is count == 0. With only a head and a tail index, head == tail can mean full or empty, the classic off-by-one. Say which you chose.
lru-cache: An LRU cache is Day 13's policy, now built: get and put in O(1), and when full, evict the key used longest ago. A dict alone finds keys in O(1) but can't tell which is oldest; a list in use order can, but moving an item is O(n). The worked example (the next step) shows the two pieces you need, a dict to nodes and an O(1) unlink; using them for recency and eviction is the problem.
LRU Cache also stores a value per key. When a node falls off the old end, you must delete its dict entry too: what must each node carry so you know which entry to delete?
get and put both move a node to the recent end, and put sometimes removes one. Which two small helpers would they share? Write those first and test them on their own.
What should put do for a key that is already there: does it count as a use, and does the size change?
Python's `OrderedDict` does it in a few lines with `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)`. Say so, then expect the interviewer to ask you to build the list yourself.

blocks.say: A circular queue is a fixed array with a head index and a count, wrapping with %; a dict from key to node plus a doubly linked list with dummy ends lets me find, unlink and add any item in O(1), which is what an LRU cache is built on.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): a browser keeps its tabs in order. Open a new tab at the end, close any tab by its id, and list the tabs in order, with open and close both O(1).
Keep a dict from tab id to node, and a doubly linked list of nodes (each with prev and next) between a dummy head and a dummy tail. A new tab goes just before tail.
Open Maps, Mail and News: head ⇄ Maps ⇄ Mail ⇄ News ⇄ tail, and the dict has 3 entries.
Close Mail: the dict hands you its node in O(1). Two lines unlink it, node.prev.next = node.next and node.next.prev = node.prev, then delete "Mail" from the dict: head ⇄ Maps ⇄ News ⇄ tail.
Open Docs: link it between tail.prev (News) and tail: Maps, News, Docs. Close Maps, the first real tab: the same two lines work, because the dummy head stands before it. No None checks.
Every step is O(1). In a Python list, closing a tab in the middle would be an O(n) remove.

blocks.title: Language models: predict the next character from counts (a bigram model), in PyTorch
blocks.builds_on: Day 8 · probabilities and cross-entropy, the log loss, Day 36 · numpy arrays, softmax, and summing each row with axis=1, keepdims=True, Day 38 · the chain rule, worked by hand on one neuron, and Day 2 · counting with dicts
points: A language model gives the probability of the next token given the ones before it. Today's tokens are single characters, and the model looks only at the one before: a bigram model ("bi" for pairs).
Mark each name's start and end with a special character ".", so ".asha." gives the pairs .a, as, sh, ha and a. The model then also learns which letters start a name and when a name ends.

Training is counting into a 27 × 27 table: row = the current character, column = the next. In PyTorch: `N = torch.zeros((27, 27), dtype=torch.int32)` and `N[i, j] += 1`, indexed just like a numpy array (Day 36), with "." as index 0 and a to z as 1 to 26.

To get probabilities, `P = N.float()` then `P = P / P.sum(1, keepdim=True)`. `.sum(1)` adds along each row; keepdim=True keeps the result a (27, 1) column, so each row is divided by its own total, like Day 36's keepdims. Without it you get shape (27,), which divides down the columns instead: a silent bug.

Sampling: start at index 0 ("."), draw the next index with `torch.multinomial(P[ix], 1, replacement=True, generator=g).item()`, move to it, and stop when you draw 0 again. `.item()` turns a one-number tensor into a Python number. `g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(2147483647)` makes every run draw the same names.

The loss is the average negative log-likelihood: for each pair in the data take −log P(next | current), then average. It is Day 8's cross-entropy with 27 classes instead of 2. Lower is better; guessing evenly over 27 characters gives ln 27 ≈ 3.30. A pair never seen in training has probability 0 and an infinite loss, so add-one smoothing adds 1 to every count first; with little data, those fake counts swamp the real ones.

A tensor is numpy's array plus gradient tracking. Make one with `requires_grad=True` and PyTorch records every operation on it; calling `.backward()` on the final number runs Day 38's chain rule backwards and leaves each slope in that tensor's `.grad`.

The limit: one character of memory can't learn longer patterns, and counting three characters of context needs 27 × 27 × 27 ≈ 20,000 rows, most never seen. Day 49 swaps the counts for a small network trained with `.backward()`, which looks at the last three characters.
blocks.say: A bigram model counts which character follows which, normalises each row into probabilities, samples by walking those rows, and is scored by the average negative log-likelihood, with smoothing so unseen pairs don't get probability zero.
example: Three names: anu, anil, ravi, written .anu., .anil., .ravi. After ".": a twice and r once, so P(a | .) = 2/3 and P(r | .) = 1/3.
After a: n twice (anu, anil) and v once (ravi), so P(n | a) = 2/3. After n: u once and i once, 1/2 each. After u: only ".", so P(. | u) = 1.
Score "anu": its pairs .a, an, nu and u. have probabilities 2/3, 2/3, 1/2 and 1. Average NLL = (0.405 + 0.405 + 0.693 + 0) ÷ 4 ≈ 0.376.
Score "arun": the pair ar never appeared, so P(r | a) = 0 and the loss is infinite.
Add-one smoothing over 27 characters: P(r | a) = (0 + 1) ÷ (3 + 27) ≈ 0.033. Small, but no longer impossible.

blocks.title: Stack: valid brackets, and keeping score
blocks.builds_on: Day 4 · stack, queue and linked list, and Day 5 · recursion and the call stack
points: A new topic, Stack. The question it answers: what is the most recent thing that hasn't finished yet? Push when something opens, pop when it closes.
In Python a list is the stack: `append` to push, `pop()` to pop and `stack[-1]` to look at the top, all O(1). Check `if stack` before looking or popping, or an empty list raises.
Each item is pushed once and popped at most once, so a pass is O(n) time, and O(n) memory when everything opens and nothing closes.

validate-parentheses: Three checks catch every bad input: a close when the stack is empty (nothing open to close), a close that doesn't match the top, and a stack that isn't empty at the end (something never closed).
A dict from closer to opener keeps the match check to one line, and a new kind of pair is one more entry.
Edge cases: an empty input, a single closer, and an input of odd length, which can never balance.
baseball-game: Baseball Game: which earlier scores can "C", "D" and "+" touch, and where are they if you keep the scores on a stack?

blocks.say: When the most recent unfinished thing matters, I push on open and pop on close, check each close against the top, and check the stack is empty at the end: one pass, O(n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): in "(a(b)c)(d)", which "(" does each ")" close? Give each closer's index and its opener's index. The input is always balanced.
Walk left to right and push the index of each "(": index 0, so [0]; index 2, so [0, 2]. Letters change nothing.
Index 4 is ")": the top, 2, is the newest "(" still open, so pop it: 4 closes 2, and the stack is [0]. Index 6 is ")": pop 0, so 6 closes 0.
Index 7: push, [7]. Index 9: pop 7, so 9 closes 7. Answer {4: 2, 6: 0, 9: 7}.
Storing indexes rather than the brackets is what lets you answer "which one". One pass, O(n) time and O(n) memory.

blocks.title: Distributed transactions: 2PC vs saga, the outbox pattern
blocks.builds_on: Day 20 · ACID transactions inside one database, Day 41 · data split across machines, Day 39 · message queues, acks and redelivery, and Day 18 · idempotency keys
points: Day 20's transaction is all or nothing inside one database. Once the order lives in the order service's database and the payment in the payment service's, no single transaction covers both: one can commit while the other fails.

Two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator asks every participant to prepare, which means doing the work, locking the rows and voting yes ("I can commit") or no. If all vote yes, it tells everyone to commit; any no, and everyone aborts.

2PC's cost: participants hold their locks until the decision arrives. If the coordinator dies after the votes, they wait holding those locks (it blocks), and one slow participant slows them all. Some distributed databases use it inside; across services it is rare.

Saga: split the work into local transactions, each committed on its own in its own service, and give each step a compensating step that undoes its effect (refund the payment, release the table). If step 3 fails, run the compensations of steps 2 and 1, newest first.

A saga gives up isolation: others can see the half-done state, such as an order "pending payment", so design the states for it. Make every step and compensation idempotent (Day 18), because queues redeliver (Day 39).

Orchestrated saga: one orchestrator tells each service what to do and tracks progress, so the flow is easy to follow and change. Choreographed: each service reacts to the previous one's event, with no central part, but the flow is spread across services and harder to see.

The dual-write problem: a service that saves to its database and then publishes an event can crash between the two and lose the event. The outbox fixes it: in the same local transaction, also insert the event into an outbox table; a separate relay reads unsent rows, publishes them, then marks them sent.
The relay may publish an event twice if it crashes before marking it sent, so consumers must be idempotent: at-least-once delivery again (Day 39).
blocks.say: Across services I avoid 2PC because it blocks while holding locks; I use a saga of local transactions with compensating steps, usually orchestrated, publish its events through an outbox written in the same transaction, and make every consumer idempotent.
example: Placing a food order touches three services: Orders (create the order), Payments (charge ₹450 by UPI) and Restaurant (accept the order).
Orchestrated saga: the orchestrator creates the order as PENDING, asks Payments to charge, then asks the restaurant to accept.
The restaurant rejects it, because it closed early. The orchestrator runs the compensations newest first: refund the ₹450, then mark the order CANCELLED.
With 2PC instead, all three services would hold locks while waiting for the coordinator's decision, and if it crashed, all three would wait.
Each service writes its event ("payment charged") to its own outbox table in the same transaction as its data change, and a relay publishes it, so a crash between the two can't lose the event.

blocks.title: Python concurrency: the GIL, threads, processes, asyncio
blocks.builds_on: Day 5 · processes vs threads, and the GIL, and Day 26 · race conditions and locks
points: First ask what the work waits on. I/O-bound work spends its time waiting for the network, the disk or a database; CPU-bound work spends it computing.

Recap from Day 5: the GIL lets one thread run Python at a time, and a thread waiting on I/O or in `time.sleep` releases it, so threads speed up I/O-bound work, and heavy computing needs processes. New today: each process has its own interpreter and GIL, so 4 can use 4 cores; data passed between them is copied, so send big chunks of work.
`concurrent.futures` gives both the same shape: `ThreadPoolExecutor(8)` or `ProcessPoolExecutor(4)`, then `ex.map(fn, items)`. Swapping one for the other is a one-word change.

asyncio runs many tasks on one thread. `async def` makes a coroutine; `await` marks a point where it pauses and lets the event loop run another task until its I/O is ready; `asyncio.gather(...)` runs several and waits for all; `asyncio.run(main())` starts the loop.

asyncio handles thousands of waiting connections cheaply, but one blocking call (`time.sleep`, a database driver that isn't async, a heavy loop) freezes every task on the loop. Inside it, use `await asyncio.sleep` and async libraries.

Races still happen with threads (Day 26). With asyncio a task switches only at an `await`, so code between awaits runs without interruption, but something checked before an await may have changed after it.

Rule of thumb: CPU-bound → processes; I/O-bound with a few dozen calls → threads; thousands of connections or an async web framework → asyncio. Recent Python versions also offer an optional free-threaded build without the GIL; the standard build still has it.
blocks.say: I choose by what the work waits on: processes for CPU-bound work, since each has its own GIL; threads or asyncio for I/O-bound work, since waiting releases the GIL; and asyncio for thousands of connections, never blocking its event loop.
example: Eight 0.5-second waits, like 8 calls to a payments API, one after another: 4 seconds.
With `ThreadPoolExecutor(8)`, each thread releases the GIL while it waits, so all 8 wait together: about 0.5 seconds.
With asyncio, 8 coroutines that each `await asyncio.sleep(0.5)`, run by `asyncio.gather` on one thread: also about 0.5 seconds.

Four counting jobs (the sum of i × i below 10 million): about 1 second one by one and the same with 4 threads, because only one thread computes at a time. With `ProcessPoolExecutor(4)`: about 0.3 seconds on a machine with 4 or more cores.
Swap `await asyncio.sleep(0.5)` for `time.sleep(0.5)` inside the coroutines: back to 4 seconds, because a blocking call freezes the loop.

blocks.title: Stack: two stacks make a queue, and what amortised O(1) means
blocks.builds_on: Days 46 and 47 · Stack, and Day 1 · Big-O
first: This block's guide reading (Résumé Mastery, about 15 minutes) goes at the end of today's HLD block, which has about 20 minutes to spare, not inside these 30 minutes.
points: Today's problem builds a queue from two stacks. The new idea is how to state its cost: amortised O(1).
Amortised cost is the cost per operation averaged over any long run of operations, even if a few single operations are expensive. It is a promise about the total, not about each call.
The counting trick: follow one item through its life. If each item can only be moved a fixed number of times, then n operations do at most a constant × n moves, so the average is O(1).

Amortised is not average case: no luck or random input is involved. Every run of n operations costs O(n) in total, but a single call can still be O(n), which matters where one slow call is unacceptable, such as a payment's deadline.
In an interview say both: "this pop is O(n) in the worst case and O(1) amortised."

implement-queue-using-stacks: Implement Queue using Stacks: decide when items should move from one stack to the other, then follow one item through its life and count how many times it can be moved.

blocks.say: Amortised O(1) means any run of n operations costs O(n) in total; I show it by counting how many times each item can move, even though a single call can still be O(n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): a list that starts with room for 1 item and doubles its room when full, copying everything across. Append 8 items.
Each of the 8 appends writes one item: 8 writes. Growing from 1 to 2, 2 to 4 and 4 to 8 copies 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 items.
Total work 8 + 7 = 15 for 8 appends, under 2 per append. The 5th append alone copied 4 items, but the average stays small.

For n appends, the copies add up to 1 + 2 + 4 + … up to the last doubling, which is less than 2n (for n = 9 it is 15), so the total is under 3n: O(1) amortised per append. CPython actually grows a list by about an eighth each time; any fixed growth fraction gives the same O(1), with a bigger constant.
Two ways to show amortised cost: add up the expensive steps, as here, or follow one item and count its moves. Today's problem suits the second.

blocks.title: Design a rate limiter: token bucket, sliding windows and a shared counter in Redis
blocks.builds_on: Day 32 · the 45-minute design framework, Day 4 · the HitCounter, a deque of recent hit times, Day 13 · Redis, Day 26 · check-then-act races, Day 6 · stateless servers behind a load balancer, and Day 18 · status 429
points: A rate limiter caps how many requests a client can make in a time window, such as 100 a minute per user. It protects servers from overload and abuse (a bot hammering the OTP endpoint) and keeps the service fair.

Token bucket: each client has a bucket of up to capacity tokens, refilled at a steady rate. A request takes one token or is refused. It allows short bursts up to the capacity and a long-run average of the rate, and stores only two numbers per client: tokens and the last refill time.

Leaky bucket: requests join a queue that drains at a fixed rate, so the output is perfectly smooth but bursts wait or are dropped. Fixed window counter: count requests per calendar minute, which is cheap, but a client can send the limit at 0:59 and again at 1:00, twice the limit in two seconds.

Sliding window log: keep every request's time, like Day 4's HitCounter, and count those in the last minute; exact, but memory grows with the limit. Sliding window counter: estimate = this window's count + last window's count × the share of last window still inside the sliding minute; two numbers, nearly exact.

Where it runs: in the API gateway, the single entry point that checks every request before it reaches the stateless servers (Day 6), so one check covers every server and bad traffic stops early. With many gateway machines, the counts must live in one shared store.

Redis as the shared store: `INCR` adds 1 and returns the new value as one command, and `EXPIRE` deletes the key when the window ends. Redis runs one command at a time, so INCR can't lose updates the way Day 26's `count += 1` did; a separate GET then SET is check-then-act and races. A token bucket's read, refill and write run together as one small Lua script, which Redis also runs as one step.

Refuse with 429 Too Many Requests and a `Retry-After` header saying how many seconds to wait, plus headers such as `X-RateLimit-Remaining`. Limit by user id when logged in, by IP otherwise and by API key for partners, with rules per endpoint (login and OTP stricter).

When Redis is down, choose: fail open (let requests through, risking overload) or fail closed (refuse, risking an outage). Most fail open with a rough per-machine limit. Each Redis call adds about a millisecond to the request (Day 13).
blocks.say: I'd put a token bucket per user or API key in the API gateway, keep the counts in Redis updated in one atomic step, refuse with 429 and Retry-After, and fail open with a local limit if Redis is down.
example: Requirements (Day 32): a UPI payments API with 10 million users; each user may make 10 requests a second with bursts up to 20, and partners get limits per API key. Non-functional: the check adds under 2 ms, and a limiter failure must not take payments down.

Estimates (Day 11): 10 million users × 50 requests a day ÷ 100,000 seconds ≈ 5,000 requests a second, about 15,000 at a 3× peak. That is one Redis call per request, which one Redis node with a replica can handle; shard by user id later.
Algorithm: a token bucket with capacity 20, refilled at 10 a second, stored per user as (tokens, last refill time) and updated by one Lua script.

A request at 1,000 ms with 3 tokens left and the last refill at 800 ms: add 0.2 s × 10 = 2 tokens, giving 5; take one, leaving 4; allow it. A user with 0.4 tokens is refused with 429 and Retry-After: 1.
Flow: client → load balancer → API gateway (limiter, Redis) → stateless payment servers. If Redis times out, the gateway falls back to an in-memory bucket per machine and keeps serving.

selftest.q: What does amortised O(1) mean, and how is it different from average case?
selftest.a: Any run of n operations costs O(n) in total, so O(1) each on average, even if a single call costs O(n). No luck or random input is involved, unlike average case.

selftest.q: Why can a fixed window counter let through twice the limit?
selftest.a: The count resets at each window boundary, so a client can send the full limit just before the boundary and again just after: twice the limit within a couple of seconds.

selftest.q: Why is Redis's INCR safe for a shared counter when GET then SET is not?
selftest.a: INCR reads, adds and writes as one command, and Redis runs one command at a time. GET then SET is check-then-act: two gateways can both read 41 and both write 42, losing an update.

selftest.q: A token bucket with capacity 10 and rate 2 a second is full at t = 0. 12 requests arrive at t = 0 and 10 more at t = 3. How many are allowed?
selftest.a: At t = 0, 10 of 12 (the bucket empties). By t = 3 it refills 3 × 2 = 6 tokens, so 6 of the 10. 16 in all.

selftest.q: CPU-heavy work in Python: threads or processes, and why?
selftest.a: Processes. Each has its own interpreter and GIL, so they use several cores; threads share one GIL and compute one at a time.

blocks.title: Stack: a stack that answers for everything in it, in O(1)
blocks.builds_on: Days 46 to 48 · Stack, and Day 17 · Arrays & Hashing
points: Some stacks must answer a question about everything inside them, such as the smallest item, in O(1), while items keep being pushed and popped.
One running variable is not enough: when the item that set it is popped, finding the next answer means rescanning the stack, O(n).
What if each entry also stored the answer for the stack up to and including it? The entries below never change while it sits above them: could its stored answer ever go stale?
Pop removes an entry and its stored answer together, and the entry below already holds the answer for what remains: nothing to recompute.
This suits any answer you can't undo by subtracting: a minimum, a maximum, a gcd. A sum can be undone on pop, so one running total would do.
Cost: O(1) per operation and O(n) extra memory for the stored answers, either a pair per entry or a second stack beside the first.

minimum-stack: Min Stack uses this idea. Before coding, say what each entry stores, then check pop, top and an empty stack.

blocks.say: To answer "the minimum so far" in O(1) on a stack, I store with each entry the answer for everything up to it, because the entries below never change while it is on top.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): a tiny markup whose tags close in order: Hi there you all!. Which styles does each piece of text get?

Keep a stack whose entries store the set of styles active at that depth, starting with [{}]. An opening tag pushes the top's set plus its own style: <b> pushes {b}, <i> pushes {b, i}, and the inner <b> pushes {b, i} again. Text reads the top: "Hi " is {b}, "there " and "you" are {b, i}.
pops, and the top is {b, i} again: " all" is still bold, because the outer is still open. A single bold on/off flag would have switched off here, which is wrong.
pops to {b}, so "!" is bold. The last pops to {}, plain text.
Each tag is one push or one pop, and the entry below already holds the styles for what remains, so nothing is rescanned: O(n) time and O(depth) memory.

first: Timer: 40 minutes. Stuck when it rings: one line in My notes on where, then take the help on its row one step at a time. Show the answer last and watch only the idea in its Video, then close it and code it from blank. Show the answer turns its bookmark on for you.
points: You built LRU Cache (Day 45). LFU evicts the key used the fewest times, and among keys tied on that count, the one used longest ago. get and put must both be O(1).

lfu-cache: Step 1, brute force: store key → (value, count, last used time) and, when full, scan every key for the smallest (count, time). What does each operation cost?
Step 2: a heap of (count, time, key) (Day 7) finds the smallest quickly, but a key's count changes on every get. What happens to its old entry in the heap, and what does that cost you?

Step 3, O(1): group the keys by their count. For each count, what structure keeps its keys in least-recently-used order and lets you remove any key in O(1)? You built one on Day 45. When a key is used, where does it move?

You also need the lowest count in O(1). The worked example (the next step) has a rule for the lowest score that carries over to a get. A put on a full cache evicts and then adds a brand-new key: in which order, and what is the lowest count afterwards?
Trace on paper first with capacity 2: put 1, put 2, get 1, put 3 (which key goes?), get 2, get 3.

blocks.say: LFU keeps a dict from key to node, a dict from each use count to its own doubly linked list in least-recently-used order, and the lowest count, so get, put and eviction are all O(1).
example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250): a quiz where each player's score only goes up, 1 point at a time. Support add_point(player) and any_lowest() in O(1).
Keep score_of = {player: score}, buckets = {score: set of players} and low, the lowest score.
Asha, Ravi and Meera start on 0: buckets {0: {Asha, Ravi, Meera}}, low = 0. add_point(Asha) moves her from bucket 0 to bucket 1. Bucket 0 still has two players, so low stays 0.
add_point(Ravi), then add_point(Meera): bucket 0 is now empty and was the lowest, so low = 1. A score only rises by 1, so the new lowest is exactly low + 1.
A new player joining resets low to 0. Today's hard needs this lowest-count trick, plus a way to break ties inside a count.

blocks.title: Machine coding: a logging framework with levels, handlers and formatters
blocks.builds_on: Day 44 · one shared object built at start-up and passed in, Day 30 · Observer, Day 16 · Strategy, Day 7 · Logger(sink, formatter) by composition, Day 26 · a lock around a critical section, and Day 21 · the machine-coding playbook and enums
points: A logging framework lets code call `log.info("order placed")` and decides, by configuration, which messages are kept, how they look and where they go. Python's own `logging` module is the real-world model.

Entities: Level, an IntEnum (DEBUG 10, INFO 20, WARNING 30, ERROR 40), so levels compare like their numbers; a plain Enum raises TypeError on <. And LogRecord, a frozen dataclass of time, level, logger name and message (Day 2).

Filtering: the logger has a minimum level, and a call below it returns at once, before any record is made. Each handler can have its own level too: everything to the file, only ERROR to the on-call channel.

Handlers are Day 30's observers: the logger keeps a list and passes each record to every one. ConsoleHandler, FileHandler and an InMemoryHandler for tests share one `emit(record)` method, and a handler that raises must not stop the others.
Formatters are Day 16's strategies: each handler holds one, so the console can show plain text and the file JSON lines without changing the handler.
Thread safety: two threads writing at once can mix their lines. Put each handler's write inside its own `with self._lock:` (Day 26), and keep the lock around the write only.
Build one logger in main() and pass it to the services that need it (Day 44), not a Singleton. Tests pass a logger with an InMemoryHandler and assert on its records.
Extensions to talk about: the time passed in for tests (Day 27's trick), files rotated by size, handlers that queue records for a background thread (Day 33), and a child logger per module.
blocks.say: My logger filters by level first, then hands each record to a list of handlers, observers that each format it with a pluggable formatter and write under their own lock; one logger is built at start-up and passed in, not a Singleton.
example: main() builds `Logger("orders", Level.INFO)` with a ConsoleHandler(PlainFormatter()) and a FileHandler("app.log", JsonFormatter(), level=Level.WARNING), and passes it to OrderService.
`log.debug("cart loaded")`: DEBUG (10) is below the logger's INFO (20), so it returns at once and no record is made.
`log.info("order 42 placed")`: a LogRecord goes to both handlers. The console prints `INFO orders: order 42 placed`; the file handler's level is WARNING, so it skips it.
`log.error("payment failed for 42")`: the console prints it, and the file gets one JSON line, `{"level": "ERROR", "logger": "orders", "msg": "payment failed for 42"}`.
In tests, the same OrderService gets a logger with an InMemoryHandler, and the test asserts that its records hold one ERROR.

blocks.title: A neural language model: embeddings and an MLP over the last three characters
blocks.builds_on: Day 45 · the bigram table, its average −log p loss, and torch tensors with backward(), Day 29 · embeddings as learnt vectors, Day 36 · a layer is x @ W + b then ReLU, and softmax, Day 42 · the training loop: mini-batches, a learning rate and an update step, and Day 10 · keeping data the model never trains on
points: Day 45's bigram model sees one character, and counting longer contexts blows up (about 20,000 rows for three characters, most never seen). A neural network can use a longer context with few weights, because similar contexts share what they learn.

Bengio et al. (2003), rebuilt in Karpathy's makemore part 2: take the last three characters (padded with "." at a name's start), look each up in an embedding table, join the three vectors, pass them through a hidden layer, and let a final layer give 27 scores that softmax turns into probabilities for the next character.

`torch.nn.Embedding(27, 10)` is a lookup table with 27 rows, like Day 45's table, but each row is 10 learnt numbers: character i's vector (Day 29). A batch of index triples of shape (32, 3) comes back as (32, 3, 10), and `.view(-1, 30)` reshapes it, joining each triple's three vectors into one row of 30. The -1 means "work this size out from the rest", so the same line serves a batch of 32 or the whole training set.
`torch.nn.Linear(30, 200)` is Day 36's x @ W + b, with W and b created for you; then `torch.relu`; then `torch.nn.Linear(200, 27)` for the 27 scores (the logits). About 12,000 weights in all.

`F.cross_entropy(logits, targets)` (with `import torch.nn.functional as F`) does the softmax and Day 45's average −log p of the right next character in one call, computed more safely. Before training it should be near ln 27 ≈ 3.3, because the network starts out guessing almost evenly.

Training is Day 42's loop. `torch.optim.SGD(params, lr=0.1)` holds the weights; each step takes a random mini-batch of 32 (`torch.randint`), computes the loss, then `optimizer.zero_grad()`, `loss.backward()` and `optimizer.step()`, which is Day 42's update, w = w − lr × slope, for every weight. Lower the rate later on.
`backward()` adds each new slope into `.grad` rather than replacing it, so without `zero_grad()` every step's slopes pile on top of the last ones. Call it before each backward.

Judge it on names it never trained on: split the names 90/10 (Day 10) and compare the validation loss with the bigram's on the same split. A low training loss alone could be memorising. The fixed window of three characters is the next limit; later weeks remove it.
blocks.say: A neural language model embeds the last few characters, joins the vectors, passes them through a hidden layer and a softmax over the next character, and trains with cross-entropy by mini-batch gradient descent; it beats counting because similar contexts share weights.
example: The name "asha" with a context of 3 gives five training pairs: "..." → a, "..a" → s, ".as" → h, "ash" → a and "sha" → ".".
Each character becomes an index ("." = 0, a = 1, …, z = 26), so the first input is [0, 0, 0] with target 1. A batch of 32 contexts has shape (32, 3).
Embedding(27, 10) turns it into (32, 3, 10); `.view(-1, 30)` joins each row's three vectors into (32, 30); Linear(30, 200) and ReLU give (32, 200); Linear(200, 27) gives (32, 27) logits.
`F.cross_entropy(logits, Y)` turns those into one number: about 3.3 before training, since ln 27 ≈ 3.30.
After 20,000 mini-batch steps on Karpathy's 32,033 names, the validation loss is about 2.2, against about 2.46 for Day 45's bigram counts on the same split.

points: Day 46's stack held brackets still waiting to be closed. Today's two problems keep the same "most recent unfinished thing" (Day 4) on a stack: for each, say what waits there, and what takes it off.
Each item is pushed once and popped at most once, so popping inside the pass is still O(n) in total: the same counting as Day 48's queue made of two stacks.

evaluate-reverse-polish-notation: Reverse Polish notation writes each operator after its two numbers: "3 4 +" is 3 + 4, and "2 3 4 × +" is 2 + 3 × 4 = 14. It needs no brackets and no precedence rules. When an operator arrives, where are its two numbers? Day 46's Baseball Game had a "+" that needed the two scores before it.

Order matters for − and ÷: say which of the two numbers is the left one before you code. And Python's // rounds down, so −7 // 2 is −4; when a question wants division that cuts toward zero, int(−7 / 2) gives −3.
asteroid-collision: Walk the asteroids left to right, and let the stack hold the ones still flying. When a new one meets the one on top, who stays? And if the new one wins, what does it meet next: is that check an if or a while?
Before coding Asteroid Collision, write in one line when two items actually meet. Not every new item fights the top: say which directions collide, and what happens on a tie.
Edge cases: one item, nothing ever meets, everything is destroyed (an empty answer), and a tie that removes both.

blocks.say: When a problem leaves work unfinished, I keep it on a stack: numbers wait there for their operator, or survivors wait there for the next item to challenge the top, and since each item is pushed and popped at most once the pass is O(n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): in "abBAcC", a letter next to the same letter in the other case cancels with it (b and B, a and A). Cancel until nothing more can go. What is left?
a: push, stack [a]. b: push, [a, b].
B meets b on top: they cancel, so pop: [a]. A now meets the a that the cancel uncovered: pop again: [].
c: push, [c]. C cancels it: []. Answer: the empty string.
Each letter was pushed once and popped at most once: O(n). In Asteroid Collision one arrival can knock off several items in a row, which is why its check is a while loop.

blocks.title: Recurrent neural networks: one hidden state carried step to step, and why long sequences fade
blocks.builds_on: Day 49 · a language model that sees a fixed context of three characters, Day 36 · a layer is a matrix multiply plus a bias, then an activation, Day 38 · the chain rule multiplies local slopes, and Day 43 · gradients that multiply along a chain vanish or explode
points: Day 49's model saw exactly the last three characters. Real text needs more: in "The tickets I booked at the PVR near my office last Friday were…", the verb depends on a word far back, and no fixed window fits every sentence.

A recurrent neural network (RNN) reads one item at a time and carries a hidden state h, a vector that sums up everything read so far. Each step: h_t = tanh(W_x · x_t + W_h · h_(t−1) + b). tanh squashes any number into −1 to 1, like Day 8's sigmoid stretched to centre on 0, and its slope at output h is 1 − h².

The same W_x, W_h and b are used at every step: one small layer (Day 36) reused, so the network handles a sequence of any length with a fixed number of weights. Drawn "unrolled", it is one copy of the layer per step, all sharing weights.
Outputs: a prediction from every h_t, such as the next character (Day 49's task), or only from the last h, such as whether a whole review is positive or negative.
Training unrolls the sequence and runs backprop through every step: backpropagation through time. The shared weights get a gradient from each step, and they are added up.

The gradient that reaches step 1 from step 50 is multiplied by W_h and tanh's slope once per step (Day 43). Factors below 1 shrink it towards 0 (vanishing), so the network can't learn from the start of a long sequence. Factors above 1 blow it up (exploding); clipping, capping the gradient's size before each update, keeps that in check.

LSTM and GRU add gates, small sigmoid layers that decide what to keep, forget and write. An LSTM keeps a separate cell memory with forget, input and output gates; a GRU uses two gates on the hidden state itself. Both let information and gradients pass many steps almost unchanged. Know the names and what the gates do; the maths isn't needed today.

Two limits stay: the steps run one after another, so training can't process the positions in parallel, and the whole past must squeeze into one fixed-size h. Attention (Day 52) lets every position look back at every earlier one directly.
blocks.say: An RNN reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state through the same weights at every step; backprop through time multiplies one factor per step, so gradients vanish or explode on long sequences, which LSTM and GRU gates ease and attention removes.
example: One number per step, to keep it small: h_t = tanh(0.5 × x_t + 0.8 × h_(t−1)), starting from h_0 = 0, with inputs 1, 0, 0.
Step 1: tanh(0.5 × 1 + 0.8 × 0) = tanh(0.5) = 0.462. The hidden state now holds the 1.
Step 2: tanh(0 + 0.8 × 0.462) = tanh(0.370) = 0.354. Step 3: tanh(0.8 × 0.354) = 0.276. The same two weights did all three steps, and the memory of the 1 fades.

Backwards (Day 38): how much does h_3 move when x_1 moves a little? Multiply one local slope per step: 0.5 × (1 − 0.462²) = 0.393 for step 1, then 0.8 × (1 − h²) for each later step, giving 0.275 at step 2 and 0.203 at step 3.

Each later step multiplies by 0.8 × (1 − h²): about 0.7 at first, nearer 0.8 as h shrinks. After 20 steps only 0.004 is left: the first input barely moves the loss, and the weights can't learn from it. A factor of 1.5 a step would instead grow to 1.5²⁰ ≈ 3,325.

selftest.q: What does an RNN carry from one step to the next, and which weights change from step to step?
selftest.a: A hidden state h, a vector that sums up everything read so far. No weights change between steps: the same W_x, W_h and b are used at every step, which is why it handles a sequence of any length.

selftest.q: Why does a plain RNN struggle to learn from the start of a long sequence?
selftest.a: Backprop through time multiplies the gradient by W_h and tanh's slope once per step. With factors below 1 it shrinks towards 0 over many steps (vanishing), so early inputs barely change the loss. LSTM and GRU gates let it pass almost unchanged.

selftest.q: h_t = tanh(0.5 × x_t + 0.8 × h_(t−1)), with h_0 = 0 and inputs 1, then 0. What is h_2?
A stack-of-survivors loop has a while loop inside a for loop. Why is it still O(n)?
selftest.a: Each item is pushed once and popped at most once, so all the while loop's pops add up to at most n over the whole pass.

selftest.q: Day 48: a queue built from two stacks moves items only when the out-stack is empty. Why is each operation amortised O(1)?
selftest.a: Each item moves at most twice: once onto the in-stack and once across to the out-stack, before it is popped. So n operations do O(n) work in total: O(1) each on average.

title: The monotonic stack · Decorator and Composite

blocks.title: Stack: the monotonic stack
blocks.builds_on: Day 35 · the monotonic deque, and Days 46 to 50 · Stack
points: Day 35's deque kept indexes with decreasing values and popped from the back anything smaller than the new item, because it could never be the maximum again. A monotonic stack is the same move with one open end: there is no window, so nothing leaves from the front.
The question it answers: for each item, the next item to its right that is bigger (or smaller). The brute force scans every later item for each one: O(n²).

The stack holds indexes still waiting for their answer. When a new item is bigger than the top, it is the top's answer: record it and pop, and keep popping while the new item is bigger. Then push the new index, which now waits too.

Why it stays sorted: anything smaller than the new item was just popped, so the new item sits on something at least as big. The waiting values never increase from bottom to top (equal values can sit together), so the first one that isn't smaller stops the loop.
Store indexes, not values: an index gives you the value (nums[i]) and the distance (j − i), and many questions ask for the distance.

Items left on the stack at the end never found a bigger item; their answer is the default, such as 0 or −1. Decide it before coding. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once: O(n) time and O(n) memory, the same counting as Day 50.
Flavours: pop while smaller for "next greater", pop while bigger for "next smaller", and < or ≤ decides what happens to ties.

online-stock-span: Online Stock Span gets one price per call and looks backwards, so its stack lives on the object between calls. What must each entry hold so you can return a span without rescanning the old prices, and should ties pop?

blocks.say: For next-greater questions I keep a monotonic stack of indexes still waiting for an answer; a new item pops and answers every smaller one, and since each index is pushed and popped once, it's O(n) instead of O(n²).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): prices [2, 1, 2, 4, 3]. For each day, what is the next price that is strictly higher? Use −1 if there is none.
i = 0 (2): the stack is empty, so push: [0]. i = 1 (1): not bigger than 2, so push: [0, 1].
i = 2 (2): bigger than nums[1] = 1, so answer[1] = 2 and pop. Not bigger than nums[0] = 2 (a tie), so stop and push: [0, 2].
i = 3 (4): bigger than nums[2], so answer[2] = 4; bigger than nums[0], so answer[0] = 4. Push: [3]. i = 4 (3): not bigger than 4, so push: [3, 4].
End: indexes 3 and 4 never found a higher price. Answer [4, 2, 4, −1, −1], with each index pushed once and popped at most once.

blocks.title: Decorator and Composite: wrap one object, or hold a tree of them
blocks.builds_on: Day 7 · composition over inheritance and abstract base classes, Day 16 · objects that share one small interface, Day 9 · open/closed, and Day 6 · trees and recursion
points: Both patterns rest on one idea: an object with the same interface as the thing it holds, so the caller can't tell the difference (Day 16's shared interface, Day 7's composition).

Decorator: wrap an object in another that has the same interface; the wrapper does something extra and passes the call on. A PriceService can be wrapped in a CachingPriceService(inner) or a LoggingPriceService(inner).

Wrappers stack in whatever order you choose at start-up: Logging(Caching(Real())). With inheritance you would need a subclass for every combination (Day 7's 2 × 2 = 4 loggers); with decorators it is one class per extra.
Order matters: logging outside the cache logs every call, logging inside it logs only the misses. Say which you want.

Python's @ syntax is the same idea for functions: `@retry` above `def fetch()` means `fetch = retry(fetch)`, a wrapper that calls the original. `functools.wraps` copies the original's name and docstring onto the wrapper, and `functools.cache` (Day 7) is a decorator you've already used.

Composite: a tree of parts where a single item (a leaf) and a group answer the same calls. The group's method loops over its children and combines their answers, recursively (Day 6), so a group can hold groups.

Examples: a folder whose size() is the sum of its files and sub-folders; a restaurant menu where a combo's price() adds up its dishes. Callers call size() or price() and never check which kind they hold.

Telling them apart: Strategy (Day 16) swaps how an object does its job, a decorator adds behaviour around it from outside, and a composite treats many objects as one. Don't add a wrapper for one extra that will never be switched off: put it in the class.
blocks.say: A decorator wraps an object behind the same interface to add behaviour like caching or retries, and a composite lets a group answer the same calls as a single item by combining its children, so callers never check which one they hold.
example: A food app's menu: `MenuItem` is an ABC with an abstract `price()`. `Dish("Paneer tikka", 220).price()` returns 220.
Composite: `Combo("Thali", [Dish("Dal", 120), Dish("Roti × 2", 40), Dish("Rice", 80)])` is also a MenuItem, and its price() sums its children: 240.
A Combo can hold Combos: a family meal of two Thalis and a ₹90 dessert costs 2 × 240 + 90 = 570, with no new code.
Decorator: `Discounted(item, 10)` is a MenuItem whose price() returns item.price() × 0.9. `Discounted(thali, 10).price()` is 216, and it works on a Dish, a Combo or another wrapper.
The cart calls price() on each item without checking types (Day 7's polymorphism). A packing fee is one new wrapper class, and nothing else changes (Day 9).

car-fleet: Sort first when the order the input arrives in isn't the order things happen in. Sorting costs O(n log n) (Day 11), more than a stack's single pass, so say the whole answer's Big-O with the sort in it.

Test one car, and two cars that reach the target at the same moment (read what the problem says about them).
simplify-path: Splitting: Python's split keeps empty pieces, so `"a,,b,".split(",")` gives ['a', '', 'b', '']. Before coding Simplify Path, list every kind of piece its input can produce, and test the shortest possible path.

blocks.say: When the input order isn't the event order I sort first, turn each item into the one number that decides things, then let a stack hold the groups or the position so far; the sort makes it O(n log n).
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): a text box keeps an undo stack. You type "dosa", type " batter", press undo, type " chutney", then press undo three times. What is left after each step?
Type "dosa": push it, ["dosa"]. Type " batter": push, ["dosa", " batter"]; the text is the stack joined: "dosa batter".
Undo pops " batter": "dosa". Type " chutney": push, "dosa chutney".
Undo pops " chutney": "dosa". Undo pops "dosa": "". The third undo finds the stack empty, so it must check before popping and do nothing.
Each edit is pushed once and popped at most once: O(n). The stack is the state so far, and the newest change is always the first to be taken back.

blocks.title: Attention: queries, keys and values, worked by hand
blocks.builds_on: Day 29 · dot products measure how alike two vectors are, and E @ E.T compares every pair at once, Day 36 · softmax turns scores into probabilities, and Day 50 · the RNN squeezes the whole past into one hidden state
points: Day 50's RNN passes everything through one hidden state, step after step. Attention lets each token look straight at every other token and take what it needs, in one step, so nothing has to survive a long chain.

Each token starts as an embedding x (Day 29). Three learnt weight matrices turn it into three vectors: a query q = x W_Q (what am I looking for?), a key k = x W_K (what do I offer?) and a value v = x W_V (what I pass on if chosen).

Scores: how well token i's query matches each token's key, the dot product q_i · k_j (Day 29: bigger means more alike). With the queries and keys as the rows of Q and K, Q Kᵀ gives every pair's score at once: Day 29's E @ E.T trick.

Scale by √d, where d is the length of each key. Dot products of long vectors are big, and big scores make softmax put nearly all the weight on one token, which leaves tiny gradients. Dividing by √d keeps the scores in a sensible range.
Softmax each row (Day 36) to get weights that are at least 0 and add up to 1: how much token i attends to each token.

Token i's output is the weighted sum of all the values. In one line: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q Kᵀ / √d) V. For n tokens, Q and K are n × d, the weights n × n, and the output has one row per token.
Every token is handled at once with two matrix multiplies, so it runs in parallel on a GPU, unlike an RNN's steps. The price is the n × n table of scores: O(n²) in the length of the text.

Self-attention: Q, K and V all come from the same sentence. In "The waiter brought the dosa and it was cold", the query of "it" matches the key of "dosa", so "it" pulls in dosa's value. Day 57 adds masking, so a token can't look ahead, and several heads.
blocks.say: Each token makes a query, a key and a value; its query is scored against every key with a dot product, scaled by √d and softmaxed into weights, and its output is the weighted mix of the values: softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V.
example: One token's query q = [1, 0], and three tokens' keys and values, with no weight matrices to keep it small: k1 = [1, 0], k2 = [0, 1], k3 = [1, 1]; v1 = [10, 0], v2 = [0, 10], v3 = [5, 5]. d = 2.
Scores q · k: 1, 0 and 1. Divide by √2 ≈ 1.414: 0.707, 0 and 0.707.
Softmax: e^0.707 ≈ 2.03 and e^0 = 1, a total of 5.06, so the weights are 0.401, 0.198 and 0.401. They add up to 1.
Output = 0.401 × [10, 0] + 0.198 × [0, 10] + 0.401 × [5, 5] = [6.02, 3.98]: mostly tokens 1 and 3, whose keys matched the query.
Every token does this with its own query at the same time: stack the queries into Q and it is softmax(Q Kᵀ / √d) V, one matrix multiply for the scores and one for the mix.

blocks.builds_on: Days 46 to 52 · Stack
points: Nested brackets mean nested unfinished work: when a bracket opens, the work outside it pauses until the matching one closes (Day 46).
The stack and recursion are twins: a recursive call pauses the caller, and the call stack (Day 5) saves its local variables for you. Any stack solution for nested brackets can be written either way.
Build text as a list of parts and join once (Day 22): `s += part` inside a loop copies the whole string each time.

decode-string: When you pause, push everything you will need to carry on later. Before coding, ask: what must you save when a bracket opens so you can finish the job when it closes, and how does the inner result join what you saved?
Numbers can have more than one digit. Check your plan on an input like "12[ab]": what should happen as you read each digit, and when is the number finished?
Say Big-O in terms of the output: "100[100[a]]" is 11 characters and decodes to 10,000 letters, so the time is at least the length of the answer.
Edge cases: brackets inside brackets, as in "3[a2[c]]"; letters after a closing bracket; and no brackets at all.

blocks.say: For nested brackets I push the outer level's state when a bracket opens, and pop and combine it when it closes; the call stack does the same thing if I write it recursively.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): reverse the text inside each pair of brackets, innermost first. What does "(ab(cd)e)" become?
Keep cur, the text of the current level. "(": push cur ("") and start a fresh cur. a, b: cur = "ab".
"(": push "ab" and start fresh. c, d: cur = "cd". ")": pop "ab" and add the reversed level: cur = "ab" + "dc" = "abdc".
e: cur = "abdce". ")": pop "" and add the reversed level: "" + "ecdba".
Answer "ecdba". The stack held exactly the outer levels still waiting, which a recursive version would keep on the call stack.

blocks.title: Quorums and storage engines: N, W, R, and LSM trees vs B-trees
blocks.builds_on: Day 27 · leader-follower replication, lag and failover, Day 41 · sharding with a consistent-hash ring, and Day 20 · indexes kept as B-trees, and what each write costs them
points: Day 27's leader takes every write, and it promised quorums today. In leaderless replication (Amazon's Dynamo, Cassandra) each key lives on N nodes and any of them can take a write: the write goes to all N and succeeds once W of them confirm. A read asks the nodes and waits for R answers, keeping the newest.

If W + R > N, every set of W nodes and every set of R nodes share at least one node, so a read always reaches a copy of the latest confirmed write. The usual setting is N = 3, W = 2, R = 2, which still works with one node down.

Tune it per use: W = N and R = 1 gives fast reads, but a write fails if any copy is down; W = 1 and R = N is the opposite. With W + R ≤ N, reads and writes are faster and survive more failures, but a read can miss the latest write.

Every value carries a version (a number or a timestamp), so a reader can tell which of the R answers is newest. A stale copy is fixed when a read notices it (read repair) or by a background sync. Day 55 deals with two writes that clash.

A storage engine is how one machine keeps its data on disk. A B-tree (Day 20's index) keeps fixed-size pages in a sorted tree and updates them in place: a read is O(log n) pages, and every write rewrites a page somewhere on disk. PostgreSQL and MySQL use B-trees.

An LSM tree (log-structured merge tree) puts each write in a sorted table in memory, the memtable, and appends it to a commit log, so a crash loses nothing. When the memtable is full, it is written out as an immutable sorted file, an SSTable. Writes are only appends, so they are very fast.

A read checks the memtable, then the files from newest to oldest, so it may touch several files; a small filter per file (a Bloom filter) answers "definitely not here" to skip most of them. Compaction merges files in the background, dropping overwritten and deleted values. Cassandra, RocksDB and LevelDB use LSM trees.

Choose by the workload: write-heavy data such as chat messages, logs and metrics suits an LSM tree; read-heavy data with range queries and transactions, such as orders and payments, suits a B-tree. An LSM tree pays at read and compaction time, a B-tree at write time.
blocks.say: With N copies I pick W and R so that W + R > N, which makes every read overlap the latest write; on each machine, an LSM tree turns writes into fast appends and pays with compaction and multi-file reads, while a B-tree updates pages in place and favours reads.
example: A shopping cart key, cart:asha, lives on three nodes A, B and C, the next three on Day 41's ring. N = 3, W = 2, R = 2.
Asha adds dosa batter: version 7 goes to all three. A and B confirm; C is slow and still has version 6. Two confirmations meet W = 2, so the write succeeds.
A read asks C and A. C answers version 6 and A version 7: the newer one wins, and C is sent version 7 (read repair). Since 2 + 2 > 3, at least one of any two nodes has version 7.
With W = 1 and R = 1, the write could land on A alone and a read could ask only C: Asha's cart would be missing the batter, because 1 + 1 is not more than 3.
Inside node A, version 7 goes into the memtable and the commit log. Later it is flushed into an SSTable, and compaction eventually drops version 6.

points: Today's new topic, Trees. Day 6 wrote a TreeNode with a value, a left child and a right child, and walked trees with recursion. Today makes the order of that walk exact.

DFS on a binary tree does three things at each node: visit it, walk its left subtree, walk its right subtree. The three orders differ only in where the visit goes: preorder is visit, left, right; inorder is left, visit, right; postorder is left, right, visit.

What each is for: preorder meets a parent before its children (copying a tree, printing it top-down); inorder of a binary search tree gives the values sorted (Day 59); postorder finishes the children before their parent (a folder's size, deleting a tree, working out an expression).
Every order visits each node once: O(n) time. The memory is O(h), the height of the tree: about log n when it is balanced, but n when it is one long chain.
Base case: an empty tree (None) visits nothing. Test on an empty tree, one node, and a tree that leans all one way.

Postorder (left, right, visit): 2 3 + 4 ×, which is Day 50's Reverse Polish notation: a stack evaluates it to 20.
Each order touched all 5 nodes once: O(n). The recursion was at most 3 calls deep, the tree's height.

blocks.title: SQL joins and GROUP BY: combining tables and counting groups
blocks.builds_on: Day 20 · SQL tables, keys and indexes, and running SQL from Python with sqlite3
points: A join combines rows from two tables where a condition matches, usually a key: `orders.customer_id = customers.id`.
INNER JOIN keeps only the pairs that match, so a customer with no orders disappears from the result.

LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table; where nothing matches, the right table's columns are NULL, SQL's "no value". Use it for "every customer, with their orders if any"; adding `WHERE o.id IS NULL` finds the customers with none.

Row count: each left row appears once per matching right row. A customer with 3 orders gives 3 rows; INNER drops a customer with 0, and LEFT keeps them as one row of NULLs. Joining on a column that isn't unique multiplies rows, a common cause of totals counted twice.
GROUP BY puts rows with the same value into one group and returns one row per group, with aggregates: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(column) skips NULLs, and SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX work on a column.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. `WHERE o.total > 300` drops small orders first, while `HAVING SUM(o.total) > 300` drops customers whose total is small.
SQL runs a query in this order: FROM and JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. That is why an aggregate such as SUM can't go in WHERE: the groups don't exist yet.
blocks.say: An inner join keeps matching pairs and a left join keeps every left row, with NULLs where nothing matches; GROUP BY folds rows into one per group with COUNT or SUM, WHERE filters rows before that and HAVING filters the groups after.
example: customers: 1 Asha, 2 Ravi, 3 Meera. orders (id, customer, total): (101, 1, 250), (102, 1, 400), (103, 2, 150).
INNER JOIN on the customer id: 3 rows, Asha 250, Asha 400 and Ravi 150. Meera has no orders, so she is gone.
LEFT JOIN from customers: 4 rows, the same three plus Meera with NULL.
Add GROUP BY name with COUNT(o.id) and SUM(o.total): Asha 2 and 650, Ravi 1 and 150, Meera 0 and NULL. COUNT(*) would give Meera 1, because her row of NULLs is still a row.
WHERE o.total > 300 before grouping leaves Asha with 1 order and 400. HAVING SUM(o.total) > 300 after grouping keeps Asha with 2 orders and 650.

points: Yesterday's recursion let the call stack keep your place in the tree. Today you keep that place yourself, in a list used as a stack. Preorder is the easiest order to start with, because a node is visited the moment it comes off the stack.

Swap the stack for a deque popped from the left, push the left child first and then the right, and the same loop visits level by level, left to right: Day 6's BFS. One data structure decides the order.
Each node is pushed and popped once: O(n) time. The stack holds the right children still waiting, about one per level on the way down: O(h) memory.

example: Practice problem (not NeetCode 250): build one string from four 3-letter pieces, "abc", "def", "ghi" and "jkl", with `s = s + piece` in a loop. Count the letters copied.
A string can't change, so each `s + piece` builds a new string and copies both parts. Piece 1: 0 + 3 = 3 letters. Piece 2: 3 + 3 = 6.
Piece 3: 6 + 3 = 9. Piece 4: 9 + 3 = 12. Total 30 letters copied for a 12-letter result: "abc" was copied 4 times, "jkl" once.

For k pieces of m letters the copies add up to m × (1 + 2 + … + k) = m·k(k + 1)/2: O(k²·m), while the answer is only k·m long. `"".join(pieces)` sizes the result once and copies each letter once: O(k·m). (CPython can sometimes grow a string in place, but the language doesn't promise it.)
When each step re-copies everything built so far, add up the growing sizes, not the number of steps. Step 1 asks you to do that count for lists.
