blocks.title: Design a key-value store: partitions, quorums, versions and failures
blocks.builds_on: Day 41 · sharding with consistent hashing and virtual nodes, Day 53 · quorums with W + R > N, and LSM trees, Day 27 · replication and failover, Day 13 · Redis as a cache, and Day 32 · the 45-minute design framework
points: The ask: put(key, value) and get(key) for terabytes of small values (under about 10 KB), heavy traffic, and always writable even when machines die. Amazon's Dynamo and Cassandra follow this design. Redis (Day 13) is the single-machine, in-memory end of it; today's guide lesson covers why its single thread is a strength.
Start with Day 32's framework: requirements with numbers (how much data, reads and writes a second, how stale a read may be), then estimates, the API, the design and the deep dives.
Partitioning: Day 41's hash ring with virtual nodes spreads the keys, and adding a node moves only about 1/n of them.
Replication: a key is stored on the first N distinct machines clockwise from its place on the ring, its preference list. Any of them takes writes (leaderless, Day 53), unlike Day 27's single leader.

Write and read paths: the node that receives a request (the coordinator) sends it to the key's N replicas and waits for W or R replies. On each replica, a write goes into the commit log and the memtable, and later into SSTables (Day 53's LSM tree).

Conflicts: two writes to one key can reach different replicas. Last write wins keeps the newest timestamp: simple, but it silently drops the other write and trusts the machines' clocks. One version number per key says which copy is newer only while writes take turns. A version number per server (a vector clock) also shows when two versions grew from the same parent without seeing each other: the store keeps both and the reader merges them, as a cart takes the union of its items.

Failures: nodes send heartbeats and gossip about who is alive, so no single machine decides. When a replica is down for a while, another node takes its writes and hands them back when it returns (hinted handoff). A node back from a long absence catches up by comparing its data with the other replicas (anti-entropy).
Wrap up with the knobs: N, W and R per use, such as N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 for carts, and what you would watch: latency, disk use and how many hints are waiting.
blocks.say: I spread keys with a consistent-hash ring, keep each on N replicas with W + R > N, write through a commit log into an LSM tree, resolve clashes with a vector clock, a version number per server, rather than trusting timestamps, and handle failures with gossip, hinted handoff and anti-entropy.
example: A ring of six machines, A to F, each with virtual nodes. hash("cart:asha") lands just before C, so with N = 3 its preference list is C, D and E, and C coordinates.
put with W = 2: C writes to its own commit log and memtable and sends the write to D and E. D confirms: two copies, so C answers the client. E confirms a moment later.
E goes down for ten minutes: F, the next machine on the ring, keeps E's copy with a note (a hint) and hands it to E when it comes back.

Two phones change the cart at once, both starting from the version C last wrote, [C:4]. C takes one change and records [C:5]; D takes the other and records [C:4, D:1]. Neither clock is ahead on every server, so a read with R = 2 returns both and the app merges them. Last write wins would have dropped one item.
D dies for good: gossip marks it down once its heartbeats stop, and its key ranges are copied to the next machines on the ring.

title: Postorder, inverting a tree, its depth · Masking and multi-head attention

blocks.title: Trees: postorder, inverting a tree, and its depth
blocks.builds_on: Days 54 and 55 · Trees, Day 6 · trees and graphs, and Day 5 · recursion and the call stack
points: Today's idea: most tree questions are answered by a function that returns the answer for one subtree. A node's answer is built from its children's answers.

It has three parts. A base case for None: what does an empty tree return? Then call the function on each child and trust it to return the right answer for that subtree. Then combine the two answers with the node's own value.
The combining happens after both calls have returned, so the work is done in post-order (Day 54). Answers flow up from the leaves to the root.

Choose the base case with care: a count or a sum of an empty tree is 0, and "every value is positive?" is True for an empty tree. A wrong base case is the commonest bug, so test on hand-built trees: empty, one node, three nodes in a line leaning left, and a full tree of seven.

Today's three problems fit this shape: Postorder Traversal is the order itself, and Invert Binary Tree and Maximum Depth each work subtree by subtree. Before coding each, say its base case and its combine step in one line.

Each node is visited once: O(n) time. The call stack holds one frame per level: O(h), where h is the height. A balanced tree has h ≈ log n; a tree shaped like a line has h = n, and Python stops at about 1,000 levels (Day 5).

invert-a-binary-tree: Some functions also change the tree on the way, and return the node so the caller can link it back in.
binary-tree-postorder-traversal: Optional step up for Postorder Traversal, once the recursive version passes: Day 55's preorder stack visits node, left, right. If you push the children the other way round, what order comes out, and what simple change to that list gives left, right, node?

blocks.say: For a tree question I write a function that returns the answer for a subtree: a base case for None, trust the calls on both children, and combine their answers at the node, which is a post-order walk in O(n) time and O(h) stack.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): the sum of all values in a tree. Root 5 has children 3 and 8; 3 has children 1 and 4.
Base case: `tree_sum(None)` is 0. Combine: `node.val + tree_sum(node.left) + tree_sum(node.right)`.
Leaves first: 1 returns 1 + 0 + 0 = 1, and 4 returns 4. Then node 3 returns 3 + 1 + 4 = 8.
8 is a leaf and returns 8. The root returns 5 + 8 + 8 = 21.
The calls finished in the order 1, 4, 3, 8, 5: post-order. Each node was visited once, and at most 3 calls waited on the stack at any time, one per level.

blocks.title: Self-attention in full: causal masking and multiple heads
blocks.builds_on: Day 52 · attention: queries, keys and values, scores scaled by √d and softmaxed into weights, Day 49 · a language model that predicts the next character from the ones before, and Day 36 · softmax
points: Day 52 in one line: each token's query is scored against every key, the scores are scaled by √d and softmaxed into weights, and the output is the weighted mix of the values. For all tokens at once: softmax(Q Kᵀ / √d) V, one row per token.

A language model predicts the next token (Days 45 and 49). In training it predicts every position at once, so position 3 must not see tokens 4, 5 and on: it would simply copy the answer. Hiding the future is called causal masking.

How: after computing the scores and before softmax, set every score whose key comes after its query (column > row) to −∞. Since e^(−∞) = 0, those weights become exactly 0, and the rest of each row still adds up to 1.

The hidden cells form a triangle above the diagonal: row i keeps columns 0 to i. In numpy, `np.triu(np.full((n, n), -np.inf), k=1)` is that mask; add it to the scores. Row 0 keeps only itself, so the first token puts all its weight on itself. Real code often uses a very large negative number, such as −1e9, instead of −∞.
Mask before softmax, not after: zeroing weights after softmax leaves rows that no longer add up to 1. Masking first lets softmax share all the weight among the allowed tokens.

One head gives each token one set of weights, so it can follow one kind of link at a time, such as which noun "it" refers to. Multi-head attention runs several heads side by side, each with its own smaller W_q, W_k and W_v of size d × (d ÷ h), so each can learn a different kind of link.

Each head gives an n × (d ÷ h) output. Join them side by side back to n × d, then multiply by an output matrix W_o, which mixes what the heads found. The total size matches one big head, so the cost is about the same.

In code, the heads usually come from one big Q (n × d) whose columns are sliced into h pieces of d ÷ h: the same as each head having its own smaller W_q. The causal mask is applied the same way in every head.
blocks.say: In a decoder, I add a causal mask of −∞ above the diagonal to the scores before softmax so no token sees the future, and I run several smaller heads in parallel, join their outputs and project them with W_o, so each head can learn a different kind of link.
example: Three tokens, "chai is hot", with scaled scores Q Kᵀ / √d = [[2, 1, 0], [1, 3, 0], [0, 1, 2]]; row i is token i's query.
Mask: the cells above the diagonal become −∞, giving rows [2, −∞, −∞], [1, 3, −∞] and [0, 1, 2].
Softmax each row: [1, 0, 0]; then e¹ and e³ share row 1: [0.12, 0.88, 0]; row 2 is [0.09, 0.24, 0.67]. Every row still adds up to 1.
With values V = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]], "is" gets 0.12 × [1, 0] + 0.88 × [0, 1] = [0.12, 0.88]. It never saw "hot": without the mask, "hot" would have taken 0.04 of its weight.
Two heads instead, with d = 4: head 1 uses columns 0–1 of Q, K and V, head 2 uses columns 2–3. Each gives a 3 × 2 output; join them to 3 × 4, then multiply by W_o (4 × 4).

selftest.q: Why does a language model's self-attention need a causal mask?
selftest.a: It learns to predict the next token at every position at once. Without the mask, position i could look at token i + 1, which is the answer it is meant to predict.

selftest.q: A masked row of scores is [1, 3, −∞]. What are its weights, and why put −∞ in before softmax rather than zero the weight after?
selftest.a: e^(−∞) = 0, so the weights are e¹ ÷ (e¹ + e³) ≈ 0.12, then 0.88, then 0. Masking first lets softmax share the whole weight among the allowed tokens; zeroing afterwards leaves a row that adds up to less than 1.

selftest.q: d = 512 with 8 heads and 10 tokens: what size is each head, and what shape comes out?

blocks.title: Trees: a tree's diameter, balanced trees, and Same Tree
blocks.builds_on: Days 54 to 57 · Trees, and Day 5 · recursion and the call stack
points: Yesterday's functions returned the answer itself. Some questions need one value passed up the tree but ask for a different one. The helper returns what the parent needs and records the real answer outside, as it goes.

The shape: the helper handles None, calls both children, uses their two results and the node to update the record, then returns the value the parent needs. Say both in words before coding: "it returns …, and it records …".

Where to keep the record: a variable in the outer function. A nested function can read it, but to assign it Python needs `nonlocal best`. Without that line, a plain `best = s` quietly makes a new local variable and the outer one never changes, and `best = max(best, s)` raises UnboundLocalError. `self.best` on the Solution object also works.

One pass, not two: if the work at each node starts another full walk of its subtree, that is O(n) per node and O(n²) on a tree shaped like a line. For each of today's problems ask: what must the helper return so no parent ever walks a subtree again, and what does it record? Then each node is visited once: O(n).

binary-tree-diameter: Say whether a length counts nodes or edges. A height can be either; LeetCode's Diameter of Binary Tree counts edges between nodes.
same-binary-tree: Walking two trees together: the function takes one node from each tree and moves both the same way at each step. First decide what happens when one side runs out before the other; that is where Same Tree is won or lost.

blocks.say: When the answer isn't the value I pass up, my helper returns what the parent needs, such as a subtree's sum, and records the real answer in an outer variable with nonlocal, so one O(n) pass does both.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): the largest sum of any subtree. Root 2 has children −8 and 5; −8 has children 1 and 3; 5 has a left child 4. The helper returns the subtree's sum (what the parent needs) and records the largest sum seen in `best` (the answer).
Leaves: 1 returns 1 and 3 returns 3, so best = 3. Node −8 returns −8 + 1 + 3 = −4; best stays 3.
4 returns 4 (best 4). Node 5 returns 5 + 4 = 9: best = 9. The root returns 2 + (−4) + 9 = 7.
The root returned 7, but the answer is the recorded 9, from node 5's subtree. One post-order pass: O(n).

Two trees, a second practice problem (not on today's list): merge tree A into tree B, adding the values where both have a node and keeping the one node where only one does. A is 1, with left child 3, whose left child is 5; B is 2 with children 1 and 4. The function takes one node from each tree.

Roots: 1 + 2 = 3. Left pair: 3 + 1 = 4; below it A has 5 and B has None, so return A's 5 as it is. Right pair: A has None, so return B's 4. The result is 3, with children 4 (whose left child is 5) and 4.

blocks.title: Builder pattern: build a complex object step by step
blocks.builds_on: Day 23 · Factory: one place that decides which class to create, and Day 2 · dataclasses and frozen dataclasses
points: Some objects have many parts, most of them optional: a food order with a size, a crust, toppings, extra cheese, a delivery slot, a coupon and a gift note. A constructor with ten positional parameters is hard to read and easy to call wrongly.

Builder: a separate object collects the parts step by step through named methods, such as `.add_topping("paneer")` and `.deliver_at("19:30")`. Then `build()` checks the rules and returns the finished object.
Each step returns `self`, so the calls chain: `PizzaBuilder().size("L").add_topping("paneer").build()`.

`build()` is the one place for rules across fields, such as "stuffed crust only on a large" or "a gift note needs gift wrap". The result can be a frozen dataclass (Day 2), so nobody ever sees it half-built.

Python often doesn't need one: keyword arguments with defaults (`Pizza(size="L", toppings=("paneer",))`) already read clearly, and a dataclass's `__post_init__` can check rules across fields. Say so in an interview before reaching for a Builder.

A Builder earns its place when the parts arrive over many steps or from different places (a search page adding filters only when the user fills them in), when the steps depend on each other, or when you want an immutable result after a long build.

Factory vs Builder: a Factory (Day 23) picks which class to create, in one call; a Builder assembles one complex object over several calls. They combine well: a factory can hand back the right builder.
blocks.say: I use a Builder when an object is assembled over many optional steps: each step returns self, and build() checks the rules across fields and returns a frozen result; for a handful of options in Python, keyword arguments and a dataclass are enough.
example: Without help: `Pizza("L", "thin", ["paneer", "onion"], True, False, None, "19:30")`. Which True is extra cheese?

Python's first answer: a frozen dataclass with defaults and keyword arguments, `Pizza(size="L", crust="thin", toppings=("paneer", "onion"), extra_cheese=True)`. Clear when the whole order is known at once.

When the order is built across screens of the app: `b = PizzaBuilder()`; the size screen calls `b.size("L")`, the toppings screen calls `b.add_topping("paneer")` once per topping, and the checkout calls `b.build()`.
`build()` checks across fields: no size raises ValueError("size is required"), and more than 5 toppings or stuffed crust on a small also raise. Then it returns a frozen Pizza.
Test: build two pizzas with the same steps and assert they are equal (the dataclass writes `__eq__`), then assert each broken combination raises.

blocks.title: Trees: the binary search tree rule
blocks.builds_on: Days 54 to 58 · Trees, and Days 32 to 38 · Binary Search
points: A binary search tree (BST) keeps one rule at every node: every value in its left subtree is smaller, and every value in its right subtree is bigger. LeetCode's BSTs have no duplicates.
The rule covers whole subtrees, not only children. Root 8 with left child 3, whose right child is 10, breaks it: 10 is bigger than 3, but it sits in 8's left subtree.

Searching: compare with the node; smaller goes left, bigger goes right, equal is found. One comparison throws away a whole subtree, as binary search throws away half the list (Day 32). The cost is O(h).

h depends on the shape. A balanced BST of a million values is about 20 levels deep (log₂ of a million ≈ 20). Inserting values in sorted order builds a line with h = n, as slow as a linked list; self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) prevent that, by name only for now.
An inorder walk (Day 54) of a BST gives its values in sorted order: a quick check, and a tool you'll use again.

Because each step picks one side, BST code is often a loop, not recursion: `while node:`, then `if x == node.val: return node`, else `node = node.left if x < node.val else node.right`; after the loop, return None. O(1) memory.
Today's problems: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST and Insert into a BST both walk down using the rule.

subtree-of-a-binary-tree: Subtree of Another Tree doesn't use the rule at all: which of yesterday's functions could you reuse there, and at which nodes would you call it?

blocks.say: A BST keeps smaller values to the left and bigger to the right of every node, so each comparison discards a whole subtree and search costs O(h): about log n when balanced, n when it has grown into a line.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): search a BST. Root 8; left 3 (children 1 and 6, and 6 has children 4 and 7); right 10 (right child 14, whose left child is 13).
Find 6: 6 < 8, go left to 3; 6 > 3, go right to 6: found after 3 comparisons.
Find 13: 13 > 8, go right to 10; 13 > 10, right to 14; 13 < 14, left to 13: found after 4.
Find 5: 8, then 3, then 6, then 4; 5 > 4 but 4 has no right child: not in the tree, after 4 comparisons.
Inorder gives [1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14]: sorted, so the tree keeps the rule.

blocks.title: The transformer block: attention, MLP, residuals, layer norm
blocks.builds_on: Day 57 · masking and multi-head attention, Day 36 · a layer is a matrix multiply plus a bias, then an activation, Day 43 · batch norm: standardise over the mini-batch, then a learnt scale and shift, and Day 38 · backprop multiplies the local slopes along the chain
points: A transformer block has two parts. Attention (Day 57) lets the tokens share information. Then a small MLP (Day 36) works on each token on its own: it usually widens d to 4 × d, applies an activation, and narrows back to d.
Residual connection: each part's output is added to its input, x = x + attention(x), then x = x + mlp(x). Each part only has to learn a change to x, not a whole new x.

Why it helps: gradients multiply through every layer (Day 38), so in a deep stack they fade (Day 43). The "+ x" gives them a straight path back, since the slope of x + f(x) is 1 + f's slope, so dozens of blocks still train.
Layer norm: for each token on its own, standardise its d numbers to mean 0 and variance 1, (x − mean) ÷ √(variance + ε) with a tiny ε, then multiply by a learnt scale γ and add a learnt shift β.

Layer norm vs batch norm (Day 43): batch norm standardises each feature across the examples in a mini-batch; layer norm standardises each token across its own features. It doesn't depend on the batch, so it works the same in training and inference, with any batch size or sentence length.

Where it goes: the original paper normalised after each add (post-norm, as in today's reading). GPT-2 and most models today normalise before each part, x = x + attention(layer_norm(x)) (pre-norm), which trains more steadily.

Attention without a mask doesn't see word order: shuffle the tokens and each one gets the same output, only in the shuffled place, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look alike. Day 63 adds each token's position to its input to fix that.

Shapes never change through a block: n tokens × d in, n × d out. So blocks stack: GPT-2 small has 12, each with its own weights, and the last one feeds the layer that scores every token in the vocabulary.
blocks.say: A transformer block is attention then a per-token MLP, each wrapped as x plus the part's output of a layer-normed x; the residual gives gradients a straight path through deep stacks, and layer norm standardises each token on its own, unlike batch norm, so it doesn't depend on the batch.
example: One token with d = 4: x = [2, 4, 6, 8]. These are Day 43's batch-norm numbers, but now they are one token's 4 features, not one unit across 4 examples: the same arithmetic on a different axis.
Layer norm: mean 5, variance (9 + 1 + 1 + 9) ÷ 4 = 5, so (x − 5) ÷ √5 ≈ [−1.34, −0.45, 0.45, 1.34], now with mean 0 and variance 1. With γ = 2 and β = 1 it would be ≈ [−1.68, 0.11, 1.89, 3.68].
Attention reads the normalised vectors of all the tokens and returns a change for this one, say [0.1, −0.2, 0, 0.3].
Residual add: x + change = [2.1, 3.8, 6.0, 8.3]. The token keeps what it had, plus a small update.
Then the same again with the MLP: x = x + mlp(layer_norm(x)). Still 4 numbers per token, so the next block takes it as it is.

blocks.title: Trees: deleting from a BST, and visiting a tree level by level
blocks.builds_on: Days 54 to 59 · Trees, and Day 6 · trees and graphs
points: BFS takes O(n) time and holds about one level at a time: O(width) memory, up to about n ÷ 2 for the bottom level of a full tree. DFS holds O(h).
Pick BFS on a tree when the question is about levels or about nodes nearest the root first; DFS for most others.

delete-node-in-a-bst: A node's in-order successor is the next value after it in sorted order (Day 54's inorder of a BST). The worked example (the next step) finds it two ways, depending on whether the node has a right subtree.

Deleting from a BST: first sort the node into a case by how many children it has, 0, 1 or 2. For each case, draw it and ask: after it goes, what should its parent point to, and does every value still sit on the correct side of every ancestor?

No children and one child are the easy cases. Two children is the hard one: two subtrees and one empty place. Ask: which value already in the tree could move into this node and keep the rule on both sides? The successor from the worked example is one candidate; why does it work?

When a recursive call might change which node sits at the top of a subtree, how does the parent find out? Think about what the function should return, and what the parent does with it. Deleting costs O(h).
level-order-traversal-of-binary-tree: Level by level: BFS with a deque (Day 6) visits the nodes in level order, but the queue holds the end of one level and the start of the next at the same time. Ask: at the moment a level starts, what tells you how many nodes in the queue belong to it? Day 6's level_sums answered this.

blocks.say: To change a BST I sort the node into cases by its number of children and check that every value still sits on the correct side of every ancestor; for anything by level I run BFS and keep the levels apart in the queue.
example: Practice problem (not on today's list): find a value's in-order successor in a BST. The tree: root 8; left 3 (children 1 and 6, and 6 has 4 and 7); right 10 (right child 14, whose left child is 13).
Successor of 3: 3 has a right subtree, so the next value is the smallest one in it. Go right once to 6, then left as far as you can: 4.
Successor of 7: 7 has no right subtree. Walk down from the root to 7 (8, 3, 6, 7) and remember the last node where you turned left: you turned left only at 8, so the answer is 8.
Successor of 13: the path is 8, 10, 14, 13 and the last left turn was at 14, so 14. Successor of 14: you never turned left on the way down, so it has none: it is the largest.
Check with an inorder walk: [1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14]. After 3 comes 4, after 7 comes 8, after 13 comes 14, and 14 is last. Each search walks one path: O(h).

blocks.title: Live updates: polling, long polling, server-sent events and WebSockets
blocks.builds_on: Day 4 · HTTP requests over a TCP connection, Day 6 · stateless servers behind a load balancer, and Day 39 · publish/subscribe, and retries with backoff and jitter
points: HTTP (Day 4) is a request and then a response: the server can only answer, never start. Live updates, such as a delivery rider on the map, a cricket score or a chat message, need the server to send when something changes. A TCP connection can stay open, so the trick is to keep one open and let the server write down it.

Polling: the client asks every few seconds, "anything new?". Simple, and any server behind the load balancer can answer, but most answers are "no" and an update waits up to one interval. A million users polling every 10 seconds is 100,000 requests a second.

Long polling: the client asks, and the server holds the request open until there is news or a timeout (say 30 seconds), and the client asks again straight away. Updates arrive almost at once over plain HTTP, but every message still costs a new request.

Server-sent events (SSE): one HTTP response that never ends, with the content type `text/event-stream`; the server writes `data: …` lines down it as events happen. It is one-way, server to client, and the browser reconnects by itself, sending the id of the last event it got. A good fit for scores, feeds and an LLM's tokens.
WebSockets: an HTTP request with an Upgrade header turns the same TCP connection into a two-way channel for small messages. For chat, games and shared editing, where the client sends often too.

The stateful-connection problem: user B's connection lives on one server, but the update may happen on another. The common fix is Day 39's publish/subscribe: each connection server subscribes to the channels of the users it holds, whoever makes a change publishes it, and the server holding the connection pushes it down.

Long-lived connections behind a load balancer: each open connection costs memory, so estimate connections per server; a crash or a deploy drops thousands at once, so clients reconnect with backoff and jitter (Day 39), and the balancer's idle timeout must be longer than the gap between messages.

To choose: polling when changes are rare and simple matters most; SSE for one-way pushes; WebSockets for two-way, chatty traffic; long polling as a fallback. Today's guide lesson (SDS 0007) covers SSE vs WebSocket for streaming an LLM's tokens, so the block's own reading is shorter.
blocks.say: For live updates I pick by direction and rate: polling when changes are rare, SSE for one-way pushes like scores or LLM tokens, WebSockets for two-way chat; connections are stateful, so I fan updates out through pub/sub to whichever server holds the user's connection.
example: A food-delivery app: the customer sees the rider move every 4 seconds, with 200,000 orders out for delivery at peak.
Polling every 4 seconds: 200,000 ÷ 4 = 50,000 requests a second, each fetching one location. It works, but it is a lot of traffic for one number.
Updates only flow one way, so SSE fits: each customer holds one open connection, 200,000 in all, spread over a few connection servers (say 50,000 each, so 4).

The rider's app sends GPS to the location service, which publishes to the channel "order:123". The connection server holding that customer's stream subscribed to it when the stream opened, and writes the event down the stream.
A connection server restarts: its customers reconnect with jitter to the others, which subscribe to their channels, and the last event id lets each carry on where it stopped.

selftest.q: What are the three cases when deleting a node from a BST?
selftest.a: A leaf is removed. A node with one child is replaced by that child. A node with two children takes the value of its in-order successor (right once, then left as far as you can), and that successor is deleted from the right subtree instead.

selftest.q: In the BST with root 8, left 3 (children 1 and 6; 6 has 4 and 7) and right 10 (right child 14, whose left child is 13), what are the in-order successors of 6 and of 7?
selftest.a: 6 has a right subtree, so its successor is the smallest value there: 7. 7 has none, so take the last node where the path 8, 3, 6, 7 turned left: 8. The inorder walk [1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14] agrees.

selftest.q: A cricket app has a million users. Polling every 10 seconds vs SSE: what load does each put on the servers?
selftest.a: Polling: 1,000,000 ÷ 10 = 100,000 requests a second, most answering "no change". SSE: a million open connections and a message only when the score changes; at 50,000 connections per server that is 20 servers.

selftest.q: User B is connected by WebSocket to server 3, and A's message arrives on server 1. How does it reach B?
selftest.a: Server 3 subscribed to B's channel in the pub/sub when B connected. Server 1 publishes the message to that channel, and server 3 pushes it down B's connection.

selftest.q: How is layer norm different from batch norm?
selftest.a: Batch norm standardises each feature across the examples in a mini-batch. Layer norm standardises each token across its own features, so it doesn't depend on the batch and works the same in training and inference.
